Joseph thus saw his descendants "to the third generation" (Genesis 50:23), meaning his grandchildren and their children.

2. In the context of generations, "third generation" evokes distant descendants: those of the grandchildren of the grandchildren. When God says that He will punish "the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation" (Exodus 20:5), He refers to those who will be born two or three generations after the guilty one—a span of time that can cover a century. This is as far as it is reasonable to count generations in ordinary human life.
H8029.origine: The Hebrew שִׁלֵּשׁ (shillesh) comes from the root שָׁלַשׁ (shalash), which expresses the idea of "three" or that which is triple. The word is formed as an ordinal adjective, similar to the French adjectives "premier," "deuxième," "troisième." It designates the rank or position in a natural order.
H8029.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, always in biblical Hebrew. It is concentrated in the Pentateuch (Exodus, Deuteronomy, Numbers, Genesis). Four of these five occurrences refer to the "third generation" in statements of God's justice: God asserts that He pursues the consequences of sin to this third or fourth generation (Exodus 20:5; 34:7; Numbers 14:18; Deuteronomy 5:9). Only once (Genesis 50:23) is it used concretely to count the living descendants of Joseph. The theological usage predominates: the word marks the limit of divine judgment on the children of sinners.
H8029.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin bears distant fruits: its consequences extend beyond the present generations. But it also teaches a threshold: God will not punish indefinitely. By setting the number of generations (three or four), divine law affirms that there is a limit to the transmission of guilt, and that each generation is not entirely crushed by the faults of its ancestors. It is a word that is both grave and tempered.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy
H8030.detail: Schilscha is a man belonging to the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Zophah and the brother of several other men: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Ithran, and Beera. His name, which means "strong" or "mighty," reflects ancient warrior values. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel, a period when the twelve tribes had separated into two distinct kingdoms after Solomon's death.
H8030.origine: The name Schilscha comes from the Hebrew שִׁלְשָׁה and literally means "strong" or "mighty." It is a typical name of ancient Israelites, formed according to the onomastic conventions of the ancient Levant. The tribe of Asher, to which he belongs, is one of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from Asher's son of the same name.
H8030.emploi: Schilscha appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 7:37, in a detailed genealogy of the tribe of Asher. This passage enumerates the descendants of Zophah, of whom Schilscha is a part. These genealogical lists in the book of Chronicles served to establish the continuity and legitimacy of tribal lineages after the Babylonian exile. His unique appearance suggests that he was a minor historical figure, with no notable event reported elsewhere in the Bible.

sens: region of Palestine near Mount Ephraim
H8031.detail: Schalischa is a region or district located near Mount Ephraim, in the central part of Palestine. Saul passes through it during his quest for his father's donkeys, before meeting the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 9:4). The name designates a territory that Saul traverses without finding what he is looking for.
H8031.origine: The Hebrew name שָׁלִשָׁה (Schalischa) literally means "the third" or "the third part." According to tradition, it could designate a region divided into three parts or a land located a third of the distance from one place to another. The exact etymology remains debated among biblical geographers, but the name reflects a territorial division of ancient Palestine.
H8031.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 9:4. In this passage, Schalischa is listed among several regions that Saul traverses during his search for his father Kish's lost donkeys. The context shows that this district was on Saul's route, between Mount Ephraim and other areas like Shaalim and Benjamin. This unique usage geographically situates the narrative and illustrates the extent of Saul's quest.

sens: The day before yesterday, or three days ago
At an earlier time, in the recent or distant past
Previously, before a notable change
Prior to a condition or event
H8032.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: "three days before," or the day before yesterday. It is a concrete expression of time in Hebrew. In Genesis 31:2, Jacob notices that Laban's face "was no longer toward him as before": there may not be exactly three days, but the idea is that something has changed since a past moment.

2. The word is mostly used figuratively to designate a vague earlier time, a time before. In Exodus 5:7, Pharaoh tells the people not to receive "as before" straw to make bricks: it refers to the habit, to what was done until then.

3. It often marks a contrast: what was so before, and is no longer. In 1 Samuel 10:11, those who knew Saul "before" are amazed to see him prophesying: the contrast highlights the transformation.

4. In legal contexts, it qualifies a prior situation that changes the judgment: in Exodus 21:29, an ox that was "previously known" to gore (that is, known to be dangerous before) makes its owner liable if it kills someone.
H8032.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁלְשֹׁם (shilshom) is formed from שִׁלֹּשׁ (shlosh, "three") and שׁוֹם (sho'm, "day"). It literally paints "three days" — probably because counting backward: today, yesterday, the day before yesterday, indeed goes back three days. This root of "three" and "day" is found in Hebrew in other expressions of time. The word has shifted from the concrete to the figurative: "three days ago" has come to mean "formerly," "recently."
H8032.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Torah and historical books. In Exodus (4 to 5 times), it describes a change of regime or behavior: what was done "before" will no longer be done. In 1 Samuel (4 to 5 times), it characterizes a spiritual or political transformation: Saul, David, once unknown, become something else. In Deuteronomy and Joshua (legal context), it helps establish the circumstances: acts committed "before" or not. In Ruth 2:11 and 2 Samuel 3:17; 5:2, it refers to past renown. The meaning varies little: it always situates a moment or state in the past to clarify the present situation.
H8032.portee: This word reminds us that time changes and that God acts in history. When we encounter "before," we are invited to see a before and an after: a divine intervention, a conversion, a break. It is a call to recognize that things are no longer as they were, and that this change is not accidental. For the reader, it reinforces the idea that God transforms people and situations, and that looking back is also noticing His work.

sens: in this place, at this location
toward this place, in the direction of this location
from this place, from there
at that moment, then
H8033G.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: "there" designates a specific place where something is located or happens. When the Lord places Adam and Eve, "there is a garden in Eden, and there He put the man He had formed" (Genesis 2:8). Aaron dies "there," at the top of the mountain (Numbers 20:28): the word simply marks the place where the action takes place.
2. After a verb of movement, "there" indicates the destination: "go there." "I will cast you... into another country... and there you will die" (Jeremiah 22:26): one is no longer simply remaining somewhere, one arrives there, one goes there.
3. "From there" or "there" at the beginning of a sentence expresses departure, origin: "From there he went up to Penuel" (Judges 8:8) means that after being somewhere, one goes to another place. It is the same root that says "I come from there." 
4. In some temporal contexts, "there" functions as an adverb of time: "then," in the sense of "at that moment in the narrative." This is a less frequent usage, but it appears when the author wants to mark a stage in the unfolding.
H8033G.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁם (sham) comes from an ancient root that expresses the notion of "place," "location." It is very close to the Aramaic word תַּמָּה (tam.mah), which has exactly the same meaning. It is a fundamental word in Hebrew: it is unclear if it has an older verbal root, as it is so elementary. The language has likely inherited this word from the Semitic stock common to all ancient Middle Eastern peoples.
H8033G.emploi: The word "there" appears more than 730 times in the Hebrew Bible, which shows how indispensable it is. It is found in all historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Judges, Kings, Chronicles) and in prophetic narratives (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It constantly serves to situate characters and actions in space: Abraham builds an altar "there" where the Lord appears to him (Genesis 12:7), Israel camps "there" near the river Ahava (Ezra 8:15). The word can be reinforced by additional adverbs ("from there" for distance, "up to there" for limit) and slightly changes color depending on whether it is used alone or with verbs of movement.
H8033G.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of the importance of concrete detail in the history of salvation. God does not save humanity in the abstract: He acts "there," in specific places, with real people and tangible circumstances. Abraham, Moses, Jeremiah — all experience God "there" where they are. This teaches us that our own life, in the place where we are today, is not secondary: it is there that God speaks to us and guides us.

sens: in this place, at this location
at this specific place (to mark divine presence)
H8033H.detail:
1. The word simply designates a place, a particular location where one is or which is being spoken of. It is equivalent to the French "there" or "here." In Ezekiel 48:35, the prophet sees the restored city and proclaims: "The name of the city will be: The Lord is here" — the word precisely indicates that place where God now resides with His people.
2. The meaning is enriched when it expresses divine presence in a place. "Here" then becomes more than just a geographical indication: it is the affirmation that God dwells there, that He is present and accessible at that specific place. This gives the word a spiritual significance: it is no longer just saying "at this place," but "God is there, among us."
H8033H.origine: The word "there" comes from a very ancient Hebrew root that simply designates the place, the location where one is. It is a fundamental adverb of the language, which opposes other adverbs of place like "here" (near) or "there" (far). The word appears very often in the Bible to situate actions or events in space.
H8033H.emploi: This adverb is very frequent in biblical Hebrew to indicate a place or situation. In the passage from Ezekiel 48:35, it takes on a particular significance: it accompanies the mysterious name of the restored city, "The Lord is here." This prophetic context transforms a simple adverb of place into a theological declaration: after the exile, the presence of God returns to the heart of the city, and this simple word "here" carries that affirmation.
H8033H.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is not distant or abstract, but that He can be "here," present at a place, in a situation, at a moment. Ezekiel's vision, ending with this word, affirms to the exiled people that the Lord does not abandon them: His presence will again be established on the earth, concretely, locally. It is a promise of return and restoration.

sens: Word by which a person or thing is designated
Reputation, glory, fame of a person
Memory, lasting trace left behind
The divine Name, that is, God Himself as He reveals and makes Himself known
H8034.detail:
1. The name is the word given to someone or something to recognize and designate it. It is a concrete sign, a label: in Genesis, God gives a name to each element of creation (Genesis 2:11), and when a child is born, they are "called" a name that marks them forever (1 Samuel 8:2: the first son of the prophet Samuel "was named" Joel). It is often an occasion to reveal something about the character or destiny of the person.
2. The name is also the reputation one acquires, the glory one builds. To make a name for oneself is to become famous and glorious (Isaiah 63:14: God led His people "to make a glorious name for You"). A renowned name is a life that matters, a trace that remains.
3. The name is a memorial, that is, what makes one remember someone after their death or absence. Keeping someone's name alive is to perpetuate their memory and ensure that what they accomplished does not fade into oblivion.
4. In the Bible, "the Name" (with a capital N) refers to God Himself, His revealed presence and His character as He manifests Himself. Praising the Name of the Lord (Psalms 54:8) is to worship God Himself in what He has revealed about Himself.
H8034.origine: The Hebrew word "shem" (שֵׁם) comes from the root that means "to mark" or "to place." A name is what "places" someone or something in a role, an identity. In Hebrew, to name is to identify, to distinguish, and thus to give an official existence. The word is used at least 771 times in the Old Testament, which shows the crucial importance of the concept of name in biblical thought: who you are and how you are called is not superfluous; it is your very identity.
H8034.emploi: The word "shem" (name) is one of the most frequent words in the Hebrew Bible, with over 770 occurrences. It appears as early as the first chapters of Genesis: God names the rivers of the garden (Genesis 2:11-14), the animals that Adam names in turn (Genesis 2:19-20), and the children who are born receive names that mark their history. As the Bible progresses, the name takes on a deeper theological significance: the name of God becomes the expression of His essence, and invoking His Name is to enter into relationship with Him. The usage varies from purely descriptive (designating someone by their label) to intensely theological (the glory and presence of God).
H8034.portee: For the believer, the name is never trivial. That I bear the name of Christian is an identity, a destiny. That I know the Name of God is to have access to His presence. That I make "a name" for myself (in the sense of glory and memory) calls me to a life that matters, a life turned towards God, a life whose trace will honor the Name of the Lord.

sens: eldest son of Noah
ancestor of the Semitic peoples
man of piety and filial respect
H8035.detail: 1. Shem is the eldest son of Noah, born before the Flood. He enters the ark with his father, mother, and brothers (Genesis 7:13). 2. Shem is the father of many peoples and nations: his descendants populate Western Asia — Arpachshad, Asshur, Elam, Lud, and Aram are his direct sons (Genesis 10:22). Through Arpachshad, Heber is born, the ancestor of the great lineage that will lead to Abraham and Israel. 3. Shem shows remarkable filial piety: during the episode of Noah's drunkenness, while Ham dishonors him, Shem and Japheth respectfully cover their father's nakedness without seeing it (Genesis 9:23). This attitude earns him a special blessing: God promises that Japheth will dwell in the tents of Shem, which means that the peoples descended from Japheth will be associated with the blessings of Shem's people.
H8035.origine: The name Shem (Hebrew שֵׁם) literally means "name." This proper name perhaps reflects the importance of Shem in the history of salvation: he carries and perpetuates the name and covenant of God through his descendants. It is through Shem that the divine promise is passed down to Abraham and the nation of Israel. The peoples descended from Shem are called "Semitic" because of this ancestry.
H8035.emploi: Shem first appears in the genealogy from Adam to Noah (Genesis 5:32; 1 Chronicles 1:4). He is then mentioned in the account of the Flood, where he enters the ark (Genesis 7:13). The episode in Genesis 9 shows him alongside his brother Japheth, respecting their father Noah. Genesis 10 lists his descendants who will form the nations of Mesopotamia, Syria, and the Levant — Assyrians, Arameans, Hebrews, and other peoples. The genealogy in Genesis 11:10 traces Shem's lineage down to Abraham, showing how the divine covenant passes through his line. These usages make Shem the living link between Noah and Abraham, and the founder of the branch of humanity through which God will accomplish His plan of salvation.
H8035.portee: Shem represents the continuity of the divine covenant and the promise through generations. His filial respect for Noah shows that biblical piety begins by honoring those who precede us. His blessing and that of his descendants remind the reader that God chooses lineages, peoples, and families to fulfill His purposes. For the Christian, Shem illustrates how God's grace is passed down from generation to generation and how obedience and respect open the ways of blessing.

sens: the word, term, or vocable that designates a person or thing
the identity, reputation, or honor attached to a person
the invocation or direct address of a person or reality ("in the name of")
the personal presence or authority of a person acting in their own power
H8036.detail:
1. The name is primarily the word that allows someone or something to be designated: this is why one asks, "What are the names of the men who are building?" (Ezra 5:4). To know the name is to identify the person.
2. The name also evokes the reputation, honor, or glory of a person: when Daniel says, "Blessed be the name of God," he glorifies God Himself and His authority (Daniel 2:20). The name summarizes who one is.
3. To say "in the name of" someone means to act under their authority, in their power, as if they were present in person: the prophets prophesy "in the name of the God of Israel" (Ezra 5:1), with all divine authority behind them.
4. The name can also represent the personal presence or essence of a reality: when it is said that God "makes His name dwell in this place" (Ezra 6:12), it means that this is where He manifests and resides.
H8036.origine: This Aramaic word is the equivalent of the Hebrew word שֵׁם (shem), which has the same root and meaning. The word comes from a family where it designates what designates, what identifies — the sign that allows recognition. In Hebrew as well, the name is linked to the complete identity of a person, to their nature, to their destiny. It is a fundamental concept: to know the name is to have a personal relationship with the one being named.
H8036.emploi: This Aramaic word appears in the Aramaic portions of the book of Daniel and the book of Ezra (texts dating from the return from exile). It appears about 10 times in these contexts. It designates either the proper name of a person (administrative identifier: Ezra 5:4, 5:10, 5:14), or the name of God in the sense of His authority, presence, or glory (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:12; Daniel 2:20). The context of the return from exile enriches it: asking for the names of the builders of the Temple also affirms that God recognizes those who serve Him. To bless the name of God is to acknowledge His sovereign power.
H8036.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of the crucial importance of knowing God by His name — not as an abstraction, but as a living relationship with His person, His authority, and His glory. Acting "in the name of God" means placing oneself under His authority and depending on His power. It also means understanding that our own name matters before God: He knows us and recognizes those who seek Him.

sens: Warrior of Israel during the time of the united monarchy
H8037G.detail: Schamma is one of the valiant warriors of Israel listed among David's companions. He is presented as the son of Ahuge, from Harar. The only biblical mention of Schamma places him during a battle against the Philistines at Lehi, where he distinguished himself by his courage (2 Samuel 23:11).
H8037G.origine: The name Schamma means "desert" in Hebrew. It is a simple and modestly documented name in Scripture, borne by this particular warrior of whom we only know this brief appearance.
H8037G.emploi: Schamma appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:11. He is listed among the "thirty" or the mighty warriors of David. The context specifies that he was a descendant of Ahuge and came from Harar. The mention focuses on an act of bravery: while the Philistines had gathered at Lehi on fertile lentil land, Schamma showed valor while the people fled before the enemy.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy
H8037H.detail: Schamma is a man belonging to the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 7:37. He is the son of Zophah and the brother of several other men of his lineage (Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Betser, Hod, Schilscha, Jithran, and Beera). This genealogical passage is part of a long enumeration of the descendants of Asher, thus establishing his place in the history of the people of Israel during the period of the divided monarchy.
H8037H.origine: The name Schamma means "desert" in Hebrew, likely evoking the arid regions of the territory where the Asherite families lived. Like many Hebrew names, it reflects a characteristic of the landscape or a quality that struck his parents at the time of his birth.
H8037H.emploi: Schamma appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 7:37, in the genealogical record of the tribe of Asher. His context is purely genealogical: he is listed among the sons of Zophah, alongside his brothers. These genealogical lists served to establish the lineage of Israelite families, particularly important after the exile to identify the true heirs of the tribal lands.

sens: King of Zeboiim during the time of the Patriarchs
H8038.detail: Schémeéber is the name of a Canaanite king of the city of Zeboiim, mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in Genesis 14:2 as one of the five kings who allied against the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah during a battle in the Jordan Valley. This king participates in the war recounted in chapter 14 of Genesis, where Abraham intervenes to rescue his nephew Lot and free the captives taken by the victorious kings.
H8038.origine: The name Schémeéber literally means "high flight" or "lofty flight" in Hebrew, composed of words evoking height and flight. This name reflects the Canaanite onomastics of the patriarchal era. Although this character is mentioned only once, his inclusion in the account of Genesis 14 places him among the political powers that controlled the ancient Levant.
H8038.emploi: Schémeéber appears only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 14:2. He is presented as one of the five Canaanite kings — alongside Bera (Sodom), Birsah (Gomorrah), Shinab (Admah), and the king of Bela (Zoar) — who unite in a political and military conflict in the Jordan Valley. This unique mention shows him as a minor political actor in the history of the patriarchal times, whose main role is to geographically and militarily situate the stakes of the chapter.

sens: Benjamite during the time of the divided monarchy
son of Mikloth
H8039.detail: 1. Schimea is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two kingdoms (Israel in the north, Judah in the south). His name means "report" or "news." 2. He is the son of Mikloth, according to the genealogical record of the Benjaminite families. In 1 Chronicles 8:32, it is written that "Mikloth begot Schimea," which establishes his place in the family lineage. 3. Schimea lived in Jerusalem with his family, as indicated by the text which specifies: "They also lived in Jerusalem near their brothers, with their brothers." Thus, he was a Benjamite established in the capital of the kingdom of Judah.
H8039.origine: The name Schimea (in Hebrew שִׁמְאָה) literally means "report" or "news," likely formed from a root denoting the action of hearing or reporting. There is a variant of the same name: Schimeam (שִׁמְאָם) which appears in 1 Chronicles 9:38, designating the same person in a slightly different genealogical list.
H8039.emploi: Schimea appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:32. He is listed in a detailed genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. The text mentions him as the son of Mikloth in the list of Benjaminite families that had settled in Jerusalem. His name reappears in the form "Schimeam" in 1 Chronicles 9:38, in a parallel genealogy of the same families. These genealogical lists show the importance of family lines after the return from exile and the reconstruction of Jerusalem.

sens: The left side of the body or a person, as opposed to the right
The left hand
The direction of north when facing east
H8040G.detail:
1. The word denotes the left side of the human body or any object. In Genesis 13:9, Abraham offers Lot a choice: "If you go to the left, I will go to the right," which shows two opposing and symmetrical directions. In architecture, the word also applies to positions: in the temple, there were five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left of the sanctuary (1 Kings 7:49).
2. The word specifically denotes the left hand. When Ehud wants to kill Eglon, he "drew his left hand, pulled the sword from his right side" (Judges 3:21) — this is an unexpected gesture since most people are right-handed, which deceives the enemy. In other contexts, the left hand simply represents a lateral position or action.
3. In biblical geography, the word can denote the north, as the ancient Hebrews oriented themselves facing east (the rising sun). Thus, when Ezekiel sees the heavenly creatures, each has a face: that of a lion on the right (south), that of an ox on the left (north), etc. (Ezekiel 1:10).
H8040G.origine: The Hebrew word שְׂמֹאל (śemōl) denotes the left side with a connotation of inferiority or weakness in many ancient cultures, including among the Hebrews. It is likely related to the root שׁמל (sml) evoking what is twisted or bent. In biblical texts, the word appears 48 times, often in parallel with "right" (יָמִין) to denote the two opposing directions or to structure sacred and architectural space.
H8040G.emploi: The word left appears 48 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily as a spatial adjective denoting a direction or position. It is used to describe movements ("do not turn aside to the right or to the left," Deuteronomy 2:27), the arrangements of religious objects (the lampstands of the temple), and precise gestures (Ehud's left hand). The word is also used in poetry to express expansion or dominance: "You shall spread out to the right and to the left" (Isaiah 54:3) signifies complete and limitless growth. In a few rare passages, it denotes the cardinal direction north (Ezekiel 1:10 with the heavenly creatures).
H8040G.portee: In the Law, "not to turn aside to the right or to the left" from the path means to remain faithful and not deviate from obedience — a call to moral uprightness. The word also reminds us that everyone has two hands, two sides: God calls us to a whole, balanced life, without exclusions. Finally, when the text mentions the expansion "to the right and to the left," it evokes the fullness and abundance of divine blessing.

sens: Direction to the left hand of a person facing forward
Left side of an object or place
North, in terms of geographical orientation
H8040H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the left side of a person: when Abram pursues his enemies after the battle, he follows them to Choba, which is to the left of Damascus (Genesis 14:15), meaning on his left while walking eastward.
2. It also describes the left side of an object or a structure: the temple has two columns, one on the right, the other on the left (2 Chronicles 3:17); it also has ten lampstands and ten tables, five on each side, on the right and on the left (2 Chronicles 4:7-8).
3. In geography, the left means north, as the ancient Hebrews oriented themselves towards the east: Samaria, the elder sister of Jerusalem, dwells to her left, meaning to the north (Ezekiel 16:46).
H8040H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of bending or leaning. In Hebrew, the left does not always carry the negative connotation it has in modern French ('gauche' in the clumsy sense): it is simply a direction in space, as objective as the right. The word regularly opposes 'right' (yamin) in biblical texts to describe the two sides of a space.
H8040H.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a precise spatial description. It is found in Genesis to indicate a military direction, and especially in 2 Chronicles and Ezekiel to describe the arrangement of the temple or the geographical orientation of neighboring kingdoms. It carries no moral charge: it is simply an indication of the left side, used alongside 'right' to locate objects or places. In geographical context, it takes on the technical meaning of 'north.'
H8040H.portee: Understanding that the left is a neutral direction in the Hebrew Bible helps the reader avoid imposing modern prejudices on the text. It also serves as a reminder that spatial precision was important for describing places of worship and the boundaries of lands.

sens: The direction opposite to the right
To turn or go towards the left side
To use or extend the left hand
H8041.detail:
1. The direction opposite to the right: the left side of space, relative to someone facing forward. In Genesis 13:9, Abraham proposes to Lot: 'If you go to the left, I will go to the right,' designating two opposing paths in the landscape.
2. To turn or go towards the left side: to physically direct oneself to the left, or to deviate from one's path in that direction. In Isaiah 30:21, the people fear going 'to the right or to the left,' meaning to stray from the path that God indicates to them.
3. To use or extend the left hand: to handle a weapon or object with the left hand. In 1 Chronicles 12:2, the archers of Benjamin shot 'with the right hand and with the left hand,' demonstrating a rare and valued ambidextrous warrior skill.
H8041.origine: The Hebrew word literally means 'to take the left' or 'to go left.' It comes from a primitive root that designates the left side of the body or space. Hebrew spoke in terms of movements and directions: to go left is to perform the action of turning towards that side. No notable word of the same family in the provided text.
H8041.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly to describe choices of direction or movements. In Genesis 13:9, it involves a moral choice: which of the two opposing paths will each take? In 2 Samuel 14:19 and Isaiah 30:21, going left or right becomes an image: straying from God's will, deviating from the path He prescribes. In 1 Chronicles 12:2 and Ezekiel 21:21, the verb describes a physical skill or concrete gesture: handling a weapon from both sides, or directing a sword's edge in all directions. The word thus oscillates between strict geographical meaning and figurative sense of deviation or choice.
H8041.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on the notion of path and spiritual direction. Going left or right is never neutral in the Bible: it is to deviate or to conform. It also teaches that God guides those who listen: there is a straight path, and side paths. For the faithful warrior (like those archers of Benjamin), mastery of both hands symbolizes a strength dedicated to righteous service.

sens: The left side of the human body or a direction
The left hand, in relation to the right hand
The west side or a lateral direction
What is located to the left of a reference point
H8042G.detail:
1. The word simply designates the left side of the body or an object, in contrast to the right side. In the purification rituals described in Leviticus, the priest pours oil into the hollow of his left hand, then dips it with the finger of his right hand: this is a precise, concrete action in a codified liturgical gesture (Leviticus 14:15).

2. The left hand appears in contrast to the right hand in the ritual: the right finger of the priest is dipped in the oil poured into the left hand (Leviticus 14:16). This is a purely physical distinction, without moral or symbolic judgment in this context.

3. The word can also designate a side of the entire body, a direction in space. When the prophet Ezekiel lies on his left side to symbolize the sin of Israel, 'left' points to the northern or western flank, a precise orientation (Ezekiel 4:4).

4. The adjective can qualify any position relative to the left in space: this meaning extends from the hand and body to general directions.
H8042G.origine: The Hebrew word שְׂמָאלִי (semali) is the adjective derived from the root שׂמאל (semaʿl), which means 'left.' This root is common in Semitic languages and refers to a basic geographical or directional notion: the sinister side of the body when facing forward. Unlike other cultures or traditions, in biblical Hebrew the word 'left' does not have an intrinsic negative moral connotation; it is purely descriptive.
H8042G.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Bible, concentrated in two very different contexts. Four occurrences are found in the purification ritual of Leviticus 14, where the priest manipulates the oil with a precision that intertwines both hands: left and right play distinct roles in the ritual gesture (verses 15, 16, 26, 27). A fifth occurrence is in Ezekiel 4:4, where the prophet lies on his left side as a symbolic act: here, 'left' designates a bodily orientation that geographically mimics the iniquity of the northern kingdom (Israel). In all cases, the meaning remains spatial and concrete, without abstraction.
H8042G.portee: This word reminds us that the Word of God governs even the most concrete details of life, from sacred rituals to the gestures of the prophet. It invites the reader not to despise the ordinary: the left hand, ordinary, finds its place in the worship of the Most High. Moreover, Ezekiel's symbolism shows how the body itself becomes prophetic language, capable of communicating the weight of sin and God's love for His people.

sens: left side of the body or space
direction opposite to the right
position or placement on the left side
H8042H.detail: 1. The word designates the left side of the human body or an object, in contrast to the right. It is a simple and concrete spatial notion: when looking forward, the left is on one's left hand. 2. It indicates a direction or orientation: to go left, to place something on the left. In 1 Kings 7:21, one of the two columns of the temple is placed on the left, and in 2 Kings 11:11, the guards surround the king on the right side to the left side of the house. 3. The word serves to indicate a relative position or a precise location: "from the right side to the left side" means that something or someone extends or is placed all around, covering the entire space.
H8042H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "left." In Hebrew, the left is often associated with what is less favorable or less honorable (in contrast to the right, which is valued), but here the word is purely descriptive and spatial. It has no complex etymology: it is a basic term of location in the Hebrew language.
H8042H.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in late texts (Kings and Chronicles). It describes each time a precise spatial position: the two columns of the temple (Jakin on the right, Boaz on the left) in 1 Kings 7:21 and 2 Chronicles 3:17, and the arrangement of the guards around the king in 2 Kings 11:11 and 2 Chronicles 23:10. The usage is consistent and literal: it always involves concretely locating a person or object in space.
H8042H.portee: This word reminds us that the sacred geometry of the temple and the military order around the king relied on a precise and structured plan. The systematic mention of "left" and "right" emphasizes that serving God and protecting the king required thoughtful and balanced organization, where every detail had its place.

sens: Benjamite, son of Mikloth
man during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
H8043.detail: 1. Shimeam is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Mikloth (1 Chronicles 9:38). He belongs to the lineage of Saul and lived in Jerusalem at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the North and the South. 2. He is part of those Benjamites who inhabited Jerusalem and remained there with their brothers, which shows that his family was established in the capital of the kingdom of Judah.
H8043.origine: The name Shimeam means "their fame" or "their celebrity" in Hebrew. It is a variant of the name Shimea (שִׁמְאָה), both formed from the root שׁמע which evokes the idea of "reputation" or "noise" (that which is spoken of). The name can also be related to Shimees, another form of the same patronymic in the genealogy of Benjamin.
H8043.emploi: Shimeam appears once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:38, where he is presented as the son of Mikloth. He is included in the genealogical list of the sons of Benjamin who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile. This genealogy traces the families that were able to return and rebuild the capital of Judah, an important step in the restoration of the people.

sens: Judge of Israel before the monarchy
Military leader who delivered Israel from the Philistines
Son of Anath
H8044.detail:
1. Shamgar is a judge of Israel mentioned in the Book of Judges, who lived before the establishment of the Israelite monarchy. He embodies one of the charismatic figures that God raised up to deliver His people from oppressors.
2. He is known for his extraordinary military feat: with a simple ox goad (a pointed stick used to drive cattle), he killed six hundred Philistines and freed Israel from their threat (Judges 3:31). This humble weapon becomes an instrument of victory, showing that deliverance comes from God, not from human strength.
3. He is designated as "son of Anath," which identifies him genealogically. His existence was so significant that his period of governance served as a chronological reference: in the time of Shamgar, the main roads of Israel had become dangerous, and travelers had to take detours (Judges 5:6).
H8044.origine: The name means "sword" in Hebrew, a remarkable irony since this judge achieved his greatest victory not with a sword, but with an ox goad. His father Anath was a Canaanite goddess of war, suggesting a mixed cultural context at the border of the Israelite lands. Despite this foreign context, God used him as a deliverer of Israel.
H8044.emploi: Shamgar is mentioned only twice in the Bible. First in Judges 3:31, where he is presented as a judge who succeeded Ehud and who, through a supernatural military act, saved Israel. Then in Judges 5:6, in Deborah's song, where his time is evoked as a period of widespread insecurity on the roads of Israel. These two references show that he ruled during a critical phase in Israel's history, marked by both external threats and a certain social anarchy.
H8044.portee: Shamgar teaches that God is not limited to human means to save His people: an ox goad is sufficient when the hand of God directs it. His example reminds believers that God can raise judges and deliverers in unexpected ways, and that the humility of the instruments does not prevent the greatness of the divine work.

sens: completely annihilate a person, group, or people
reduce to nothing, make disappear without a trace
devastate, ravage a place or its inhabitants
end the existence of something through violence or domination
erase, eliminate all memory or vestige
H8045.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the complete annihilation of a people or nation. When God says, "I will destroy them," it is a radical and definitive removal of those peoples. In Deuteronomy 9:3, the Lord "will destroy" the Canaanite nations before Israel, which means eliminating them as an obstacle to the possession of the land.
2. Sometimes the word describes total disappearance and the void of memory: in Isaiah 26:14, God has "destroyed" His enemies and "eliminated all memory" of them, which shows that to destroy is not only to kill, but to erase even the trace.
3. It also expresses the devastation of a territory or the extermination of a household: in Genesis 34:30, Jacob fears being "destroyed," he and his household, meaning his clan completely annihilated.
4. The word can also denote an act of domination and crushing: in 2 Samuel 21:5, Saul wanted to destroy Israel from the territory, to completely crush it.
5. Sometimes it carries the idea of a planned and deliberate destruction: in Esther 4:8, the decree of destruction aims to systematically exterminate the Jews.
H8045.origine: The root שׁמד (shamad) expresses the fundamental idea of reducing to nothing, annihilating. It is attested in Hebrew and Aramaic (where it has the same form and meaning), which shows its antiquity and weight in both Semitic languages. The verb is mostly used in the Niphal (passive or reflexive form: "to be destroyed") and in the Hiphil (causative form: "to cause to be destroyed, annihilate"), two ways of showing that destruction is a complete process, either suffered or deliberately inflicted.
H8045.emploi: The verb shamad appears 86 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in Deuteronomy (where it describes the destructions that God orders or threatens), the historical books (where it recounts wars and vengeance), and the Psalms and Prophets (where it evokes divine judgment). In Deuteronomy, it is almost always used to threaten or describe the elimination of the Canaanite peoples or the annihilation of Israel if it disobeys (Deuteronomy 7:24, 9:3, 31:3-4). In Esther, it designates the systematic plan for the extermination of the Jews. In the prophets like Isaiah, it expresses God's radical judgment against enemies and the annihilation of their memory. The word changes little in meaning between these contexts: it is always about complete and definitive elimination.
H8045.portee: This word reminds us of the terrifying reality of divine judgment: God does not only threaten to punish, but to radically annihilate those who resist Him or oppress His people. For the Christian reader, it invites us to take seriously both God's mercy towards Israel (He has destroyed His enemies) and the gravity of sin (He threatens to destroy those who reject Him). This word calls us to faithfulness through reverential fear and not through indifference.

sens: completely annihilate something, make it disappear without a trace
suppression of an authority or political power
H8046.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of reducing to nothing, making something completely disappear. In Daniel 7:26, it refers to the dominion of the kingdom that will be "destroyed" — not only defeated but annihilated in a definitive and irreversible manner, with no possibility of restoration.
2. The political sense is clearly evident when this verb applies to an authority: it is the radical suppression of power and dominion, like the fall of an empire whose grip is eradicated even to the memory.
H8046.origine: The Aramaic word שְׁמַד (shemod) comes from the same Hebrew root שָׁמַד (shamad) which literally means "to destroy" or "to annihilate." The root evokes the image of total and irreversible destruction. This root exists in several Semitic languages with the same meaning. The Aramaic word is used here in the Aphel form, which intensifies the action: it is a complete and caused destruction.
H8046.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic Bible (Daniel 7:26). It describes a major eschatological event: the definitive destruction of the dominion of an apocalyptic beast and the establishment of divine judgment. The context shows that this destruction is irrevocable — it will not be followed by restoration. It is a strong term, reserved for events of cosmic and undeniable significance.
H8046.portee: This verb reminds the reader that God controls history down to its ultimate ends. No earthly power, no matter how powerful, can escape divine judgment. The destruction announced in Daniel 7:26 assures the believer that the kingdoms opposing God will ultimately be annihilated, while God's eternal reign will be established without question.

sens: State of ruin and abandonment of a once inhabited place
Terror and horror caused by destruction
Act of devastating, reducing to ruins
H8047G.detail:
1. Desolation is primarily the physical state of a territory or city reduced to ruins and abandoned by its inhabitants. It is the spectacle of destruction: empty lands, cities in ruins, absence of life. Jeremiah describes how the land will become "a ruin, a desert" under divine judgment (Jeremiah 25:11), an image from Isaiah where "devastation remains in the city" after destruction (Isaiah 24:12).

2. The word also denotes the feeling of horror and dread caused by this destruction. It is the moral and spiritual impoverishment that accompanies annihilation: the inhabitants will be "an object of horror and curse" (2 Kings 22:19), an expression of consternation in the face of divine judgment.

3. Sometimes the word describes the very act of devastating, the work of destruction. Psalms 73:19 speaks of the wicked being "destroyed" in an instant, suddenly annihilated by the power of God.
H8047G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning to be desolate, to be horrified. It is related to the idea of emptiness, absence, complete upheaval. Desolation evokes a landscape emptied of its inhabitants, a heavy silence after violence, the palpable horror of a completed judgment.
H8047G.emploi: This term appears 22 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the prophets (notably Jeremiah). It primarily designates God's judgment on the nations and on Judah: Jeremiah, Isaiah, and the other prophets use it to announce the ruin that will come upon Jerusalem and the enemies of Israel. The context is always that of divine punishment: desolation comes because of unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 44:22) and sin. It thus carries a strong theological dimension: it is not a mere natural disaster, but the result of the Lord's judgment.
H8047G.portee: Desolation reminds the believer of the reality of divine judgment and the seriousness of sin. It teaches that unfaithfulness to God inevitably leads to destruction. For the Christian, it invites a fear of God and a respect for His word. It is also a warning: the absence of God, the spiritual void, is not a neutral state, but a consequence of judgment.

sens: A land, a city completely ravaged, in ruins
The horror and disgust provoked by this destruction
The dread and astonishment of witnesses facing a spectacle of ruins
That which causes dread and repugnance, that which is abominable
H8047H.detail:
1. A land or city in ruins, abandoned, transformed into rubble: it is the physical state of a region devastated by war or divine judgment. Jeremiah 25:9 speaks of a land reduced to "an object of desolation and mockery, eternal ruins."
2. The horror and disgust inspired by this destruction: the feeling of repulsion before a spectacle of ruin and devastation. Jeremiah 5:30 says, "Horrible, abominable things are done in the land."
3. The dread and astonishment felt by those who see these ruins: Jeremiah 18:16 describes how "All who pass by are astonished and shake their heads."
4. That which provokes repugnance and fear, that which is morally repugnant or disgusting. Deuteronomy 28:37 warns that Israel will become "an object of astonishment, sarcasm, and ridicule"—a spectacle that horrifies other peoples.
H8047H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be desolate, to be reduced to ruins." It expresses the idea of complete destruction that leaves behind a landscape empty and horrible. The word belongs to the vocabulary of divine judgment: when God abandons a people, He transforms their land into desolation.
H8047H.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the prophet Jeremiah (13 occurrences). It always describes a major destruction, either of a city or an entire people struck by divine judgment. The Babylonians will ravage Jerusalem and make it desolate (Jeremiah 25:9, 29:18); Egypt will also be desolate if it refuses to obey God (Jeremiah 42:18). The word is often coupled with "mockery" or "reproach": desolation is not merely a material ruin, it is a public humiliation. In Jeremiah 18:16, those who see the ruins "shake their heads"—the visible sign of horror and judgment.
H8047H.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment is not an abstract theory: it is a destructive reality, visible, that transforms lands and cities into ruins. For the readers of Jeremiah, this warning was urgent: refusing God does not bring hidden blessing, but public and lasting desolation. For us, it is a call to spiritual vigilance: what are the "desolations" we see around us? And how should this thought of judgment lead us to humility and obedience?

sens: Son of Reuel and grandson of Esau, Edomite chief
H8048G.detail: Shamma is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the lineage of Esau. He is the son of Reuel (who is himself the son of Esau) and is listed among the chiefs of the people of Edom. The Bible mentions him three times, always in the context of Esau's genealogy: in Genesis 36:13, where he is listed with his brothers Nahath, Zerah, and Mizza as the sons of Reuel; in Genesis 36:17, where he is explicitly designated as a chief in the land of Edom; and in 1 Chronicles 1:37, where the genealogical list is repeated. These passages show that Shamma held a position of responsibility among the people of Edom, the cousin of Israel by blood.
H8048G.origine: The name Shamma means "astonishment" or "stupor" in Hebrew. It designates in the Bible a representative of the Edomite line, the descendants of Esau who became a neighboring and rival nation to Israel. The genealogical context shows that Shamma was part of the ruling elite of Edom during the patriarchal times.
H8048G.emploi: Shamma appears exclusively in the genealogical passages of Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1, which list the descendants of Esau and the chiefs of Edom. He is mentioned only three times, always alongside his brothers Nahath, Zerah, and Mizza, and identified as the son of Reuel and grandson of Esau. The text of Genesis 36:17 explicitly designates him as chief ("chief Shamma"), indicating that he exercised political or administrative authority in the kingdom of Edom. His name appears in the two main genealogical sources of the Old Testament, confirming his importance in the Edomite lineage.

sens: Elite warrior of King David
Son of Reuel and grandson of Esau
Brother of King David
H8048H.detail:
1. Schamma is a warrior who ranks among the 30 most renowned warriors of King David, a group of formidable men who formed the military elite of Israel (2 Samuel 23:25). He is referred to as "of Harod," which likely indicates his city of origin or his connection to a region.

2. Schamma bears a name that means "astonishment" or "desolation," perhaps alluding to the effect of fear that his presence caused in battle. He is a descendant of Esau through his father Reuel, placing him in the royal genealogy of Edom.
H8048H.origine: The name Schamma comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be desolate" or "to be struck with astonishment." This original meaning evokes the idea of amazement or terror in the face of something impressive. The same character is also named Schammoth (with a slightly different ending) in the parallel account of 1 Chronicles 11:27, showing that ancient scribes preserved multiple forms of the same name.
H8048H.emploi: Schamma appears in the register of David's 30 warriors, in 2 Samuel 23:25. This passage, which lists the most courageous and experienced men of King David, holds great historical significance: it documents the military companions of the great king of Israel during the period of the united kingdom. Schamma is identified as "of Harod," distinguishing him from other warriors with a similar name.
H8048H.portee: Schamma reminds us that the ministry of a man of God like David relied on devoted, courageous, and loyal men. These warriors embody the value of loyal service and dedication to the cause of the Lord. For the believer, this register shows that God honors and recognizes those who give themselves wholeheartedly to the service of His plans.

sens: One of the thirty elite warriors of King David
A Hararite, renowned warrior
H8048I.detail:
1. Schamma is a warrior who ranks among the thirty most valiant men of King David. The Bible designates him in Greek by the term "Shammah," a name that etymologically means "astonishment" or "desolation." He belongs to this elite group of fighters who served David during his years of reign.
2. He is specifically qualified as a Hararite, meaning he is from Harar (or the mountainous region of the Hara). This geographical origin distinguishes his lineage among the other warriors of David listed in the roll of champions.
H8048I.origine: The name Schamma (שַׁמָּה in Hebrew) literally means "astonishment" or "desolation." Its etymology evokes the idea of being struck with astonishment or amazement, which perhaps underscores the powerful impression this renowned warrior must have made. He is also called "Shagée" (שָׁגֵה) in another list, two names that likely refer to the same character in different biblical texts.
H8048I.emploi: Schamma is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the second book of Samuel, in the catalog of the thirty elite warriors of King David (2 Samuel 23:33). He is presented there as a man of great valor, worthy of standing alongside the bravest fighters of Israel. This brief mention places Schamma in the context of David's court and army at the height of his power, during the days of the united monarchy of Israel.
H8048I.portee: The memory of Schamma in the Scriptures reminds us that God has always blessed His people with men of worth and courage. These warriors, who appear in the register of the "thirty," symbolize the faithfulness and dedication of the men who supported the reign of King David. For today's believer, this is an invitation to recognize that God highlights the faithful and the courageous who serve with honor.

sens: Son of Jesse and brother of David
H8048J.detail: Schamma is one of the sons of Jesse, the father of David. He is the third eldest son of Jesse mentioned in the account of David's anointing by the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 16:9; 17:13). In this famous scene, Samuel examines Jesse's sons to find the one whom God has chosen to be king in place of Saul, and Schamma is among those presented but rejected. He accompanies Saul to war alongside his brothers Eliab and Abinadab.
H8048J.origine: The name Schamma means "astonishment" or "amazement" in Hebrew. It is a typical proper name from the ancient Near East. This name also appears in other forms: Shimea (in the text of 1 Chronicles 2:13 and 20:7) and Shimeah, variants that designate the same character in different biblical texts.
H8048J.emploi: Schamma appears in the context of David's royal family during the time of the united monarchy of Israel. He is mentioned twice: first in 1 Samuel 16:9, where Samuel passes him over without choosing him, and then in 1 Samuel 17:13, where he is again cited among the three eldest sons of Jesse who followed Saul to war. Although he is an important member of David's family and the clan of Jesse, the Bible reports nothing particular about his deeds or personal life; he remains a secondary figure in the biblical narrative.

sens: A military chief during the time of King David
H8049.detail: Schamehuth was one of the twelve officers responsible for organizing the royal army under King David's reign. He specifically commanded the fifth monthly division, meaning he was responsible for the order and discipline of the troops during the fifth month of the year (1 Chronicles 27:8). Each month, a division of twenty-four thousand men was entrusted to him — a structure that ensured a stable and rotating military presence throughout the year.
H8049.origine: The Hebrew name Schamehuth literally means "desolation." It shares its root with the word "desolate" or "ruined." This name may seem strange for a warrior, but ancient Hebrews sometimes gave their children names evoking difficult situations or experiences from the time of their birth. The biblical text also mentions him under variations: "Shammoth" and "Shammah."
H8049.emploi: Schamehuth appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:8. He is listed in the official roster that David established to organize the military administration of the kingdom at its various levels. This passage enumerates the twelve division chiefs who took turns each month of the year. Schamehuth is presented as "the Jizrachite" — meaning a man from Jezreel — indicating his region of origin. His sole mention shows that he was a trusted officer, worthy of being recorded in the royal archives.

sens: Prophet and judge of Israel during the time of Saul and David
The one whom God hears or whose name means 'his name is God'
H8050G.detail:
1. Samuel is the prophet and judge whom Israel listened to at the end of the period of the judges and the beginning of the monarchy (1 Samuel 1:20). He was born from the fervent prayer of his mother Hannah, who dedicated him to God from his childhood at the tabernacle in Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:18). God spoke to him and made him known as a prophet throughout Israel (1 Samuel 3:20). Samuel publicly intervened to call Israel back to the Lord, winning a victory against the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:9-10), and he judged Israel for a long time before establishing Saul and then David as kings (1 Samuel 9:15, 1 Samuel 16:13).
2. The name Samuel means 'his name is God' or 'God hears', reflecting that the mother of a long-awaited child saw in him a divine answer to her supplication.
H8050G.origine: The Hebrew name שְׁמוּאֵל (Shemuel) is composed of two elements: 'shém' (name) and 'El' (God). It literally means 'his name is God' or can be understood as 'God hears'. It is a theophoric name, composed of the divine name, common in the Bible to express a close relationship with God or a divine invocation. The name expresses that God heard Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1:20).
H8050G.emploi: Samuel appears 134 times in the Bible, mostly in the book of 1 Samuel and the beginning of 2 Samuel, as well as in 1 Chronicles. He is the central prophet who connects the period of the judges to that of the Israelite monarchy. From his childhood at the tabernacle (1 Samuel 3:4-10), he receives visions from God and becomes the spokesperson of the Lord. The people ask him to pray for them (1 Samuel 7:5-8), he convenes the assemblies of Israel (1 Samuel 10:17), anoints kings (1 Samuel 10:1, 1 Samuel 16:13), and corrects those who stray from God, notably Saul (1 Samuel 15:10-17). His words carry prophetic authority: 'the word of Samuel came to all Israel' (1 Samuel 4:1).
H8050G.portee: Samuel embodies the faithful prophet who remains committed to the word of God and the well-being of the people, even when they reject him. His life shows how God can speak to a consecrated child and entrust him with a mission of spiritual and political liberation. For the believer, Samuel reminds us that God hears sincere prayer and raises up servants to lead His people to Him.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Simeon, tasked with dividing the territory of Canaan
H8050H.detail: Samuel (the name means 'his name is God') is here a tribal chief designated to participate in the distribution of the lands promised to the Israelites after their entry into Canaan. He is the son of Ammihud and represents the tribe of Simeon during this solemn distribution (Numbers 34:20).
H8050H.origine: The name Samuel comes from Hebrew and literally means 'his name is God' or 'God has heard'. It is a theophoric name, which expresses a relationship with God. The same name was borne by the most famous prophet and judge of Israel, son of Elkanah and Hannah, who lived much later during the days of Saul and David.
H8050H.emploi: This Samuel appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:20, where he is named among the tribal leaders chosen to oversee the division of the territory of Canaan among the twelve tribes. He lived during the time of the Exodus from Egypt and the wilderness period. He should be distinguished from the prophet and judge Samuel, who is a much more significant figure appearing throughout the books of 1 Samuel.

sens: Son of Tola and grandson of Issachar
H8050I.detail: Samuel is a man from the tribe of Issachar mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 7:2. He is the son of Tola and the brother of Uzzi, Rephiah, Jeriel, Jachmaï, and Jibsam—all heads of families in their generation. This ancestor of Israel is noted among the 'valiant men' of his time, during the reign of King David.
H8050I.origine: The name Samuel literally means 'His Name is God' or 'God has heard', composed of the Hebrew word for 'name' and the divine name 'El'. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within itself, which was common among the Hebrews to express a particular relationship with the Lord.
H8050I.emploi: This Samuel is one of three characters bearing this name in the Hebrew Bible. Unlike the prophet Samuel, son of Elkanah and Hannah, who played a major role during the times of Saul and David, this one is simply a genealogist noted in the register of the tribe of Issachar. He appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 7:2, in the genealogical list of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Reuben sent as a scout to Canaan
H8051G.detail: 1. Schammua is one of the twelve men that Moses sends to explore the land of Canaan before the conquest. He represents the tribe of Reuben and reports with his companions the news of the promised land (Numbers 13:4).
H8051G.origine: The name Schammua means 'renowned' or 'famous' in Hebrew. It is a compound name expressing the idea of reputation and recognition.
H8051G.emploi: Schammua appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:4, where he is presented as the son of Zaccur and the representative of the tribe of Reuben among the twelve spies. His name is listed among the trustworthy men chosen for this decisive mission. There are other characters with the same or a similar name (notably a son of David), but this text specifically designates this Schammua of Reuben.

sens: Son of David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem
H8051H.detail: 1. Schammua is one of the sons that David had with Bathsheba in Jerusalem. He appears in the list of children born to David during his reign, listed alongside his brothers Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. His name means 'the renowned' or 'he who has a good reputation'. He is mentioned twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages that provide the same inventory of David's sons.
H8051H.origine: The name Schammua (שַׁמּוּעַ in Hebrew) literally means 'he who is renowned' or 'the famous', composed of a root evoking celebrity and fame. In the Chronicles, this same character is sometimes called Shimea (שִׁמְעָה), a variant of the same name. It is a typical name from the Davidic era, borne by several characters in the Old Testament.
H8051H.emploi: Schammua is mentioned only twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages: in 2 Samuel 5:14 and in 1 Chronicles 14:4, both of which list the children born to David in Jerusalem. He is included in the list of the four sons he had with Bathsheba: Schammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. Solomon, the youngest of these brothers, will become the king who succeeds David. Schammua himself plays no active role reported in the biblical narrative; he is simply named as a member of the Davidic royal family.

sens: Priest of the return from exile
Head of a priestly family
H8051I.detail:
1. Schammua is a priest who lived during the return from the exile of Israel (around the 5th century B.C.), at the time of Nehemiah. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:18.
2. He is the head (or representative) of the priestly family of Bilgah, one of the twenty-four families of priests who served at the temple in Jerusalem. His name means 'famous' or 'renowned' in Hebrew.
H8051I.origine: The name 'Schammua' comes from a Hebrew root evoking celebrity or fame. It is a late theophoric name, borne by several characters in the Old Testament, including a son of King David. The name here designates a priest of the return from exile, at a time when such names remained common in Levitical families.
H8051I.emploi: Schammua is mentioned only once in Nehemiah 12:18, in the official list of priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel from exile in Babylon and who inhabited Jerusalem. He appears as the head of the paternal house of Bilgah, one of the sections of the priesthood. This mention shows that he held a position of responsibility within the cultic organization of the restored temple, around the 5th century B.C.

sens: Levite of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, father of Abda
H8051J.detail: Schammua is a man from the tribe of Levi mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:17, where he is presented as the father of Abda. These two men are part of the Levites who resettled in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. Abda, son of Schammua, is specifically mentioned for his important role in worship: his son participates in the praise and prayer of the restored temple. Schammua thus represents a generation of Levites who contributed to the reconstruction of the religious community of Israel after the exile.
H8051J.origine: The name Schammua means "renowned" or "famous" in Hebrew. It is formed from a root that evokes the notion of making oneself known or leaving a name. This name appears in several Levitical and priestly genealogies in the Old Testament, carrying the idea of an established reputation or family recognition.
H8051J.emploi: Schammua is mentioned only once in Nehemiah 11:17, in the context of the genealogical list of Levites who returned from captivity and resided in Jerusalem. This list in Nehemiah 11 documents the resumption of organized life for the Hebrew people after the exile, with the establishment of priests and Levites in their respective religious functions. The name appears in the ascending genealogy of Abda, which shows the importance of the Levite lineages in the religious organization of restored Judea.

sens: A message, information, news that reaches someone
A rumor that spreads
A reputation, what is said or told about someone
The mention, the fact that something is brought up or reported
H8052.detail:
1. A news is a message that arrives: it is information, good or bad, that comes to you from afar or elsewhere. When Joab learns that King Solomon has put a price on his head, "the news reached Joab" (1 Kings 2:28): a news has spread to him. 
2. A rumor that circulates from one person to another and spreads: it is what is said, what is heard. Isaiah speaks of "his news" which alone brings terror (Isaiah 28:19), meaning the news that spreads creates panic. 
3. A reputation, what is publicly said about someone or their reputation: the queen of Sheba heard about Solomon's wisdom, "and there was more news" than what she had learned (1 Kings 10:7 implicit in the usages). 
4. The fact that something is mentioned, that something is talked about: when Ezekiel asks "did you not speak of your sister Sodom?" (Ezekiel 16:56), it refers to the words, the mentions that were made about it.
H8052.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to hear, to listen." A news is primarily what is heard, what arrives at the ears. The word emphasizes that information depends on transmission, on what is said and heard around you. It is a very spoken word, evoking the living process of rumors and information circulating in a group or region.
H8052.emploi: This word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the prophetic and historical books. It designates either a concrete news (the arrival of a troop, Jeremiah 49:14; the death of a child, 2 Samuel 4:4), or a rumor that causes fear (Jeremiah 51:46 mentions "news that circulated") or that encourages (Psalms 112:7: the one who fears God "does not fear bad news"). It can also be a bad reputation: when David learns that his own words cause the people to sin, it is a "bad news" he hears (1 Samuel 2:24). The Segond translates as "new," "noise," "news," "reputation" depending on the context.
H8052.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what circulates around them and on how words and information propagate. The one who fears God is not enslaved by the fear sown by bad news (Psalms 112:7), because their heart rests on the Lord. It is a lesson in trust: in a world full of noise and rumors, the believer learns not to be dominated by what they hear, but to keep their gaze turned toward God.

sens: Elite warrior of King David
H8054.detail: Schammoth is one of the thirty most valiant warriors in the service of King David. He is from Haror and appears in the list of military champions of the united kingdom of Israel (1 Chronicles 11:27).
H8054.origine: The name Schammoth means "desolations" in Hebrew. It is a variant or another name for Schamma (mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:25), one of David's renowned warriors. This name may evoke places or events marked by destruction, although the historical character is a faithful and strong fighter.
H8054.emploi: Schammoth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:27, in the list of David's thirty elite warriors. He is identified as being from Haror and belongs to the group of men most renowned for their military valor. This list celebrates David's faithful during the united kingdom and shows the importance of trustworthy warriors in the organization of royal power.
H8054.portee: This name reminds us that God raises up courageous and faithful men to serve His purposes and protect His people. David's warriors symbolize strength put at the service of the king's justice and, by extension, of God Himself.

sens: To experience a lively joy, a satisfaction of the heart
To express this joy through words or gestures
To find pleasure, satisfaction in something
To rejoice in God, finding in Him deep joy
H8055.detail:
1. To rejoice is to experience a joy that rises from the heart and fills it. Aaron "rejoiced" in his heart upon learning that Moses was coming (Exodus 4:14): it is a sincere inner feeling. It is the opposite of sadness, mourning, discouragement.

2. This joy is expressed and manifested: the righteous "rejoice" in the Lord and "shout for joy" (Psalms 32:11). The word also designates the act of rejoicing together, celebrating: one rejoices during religious festivals, at harvest time (Deuteronomy 12:7).

3. To rejoice is also to take pleasure in something particular: what pleases the eyes rejoices the heart (Proverbs 15:30). It is to experience satisfaction, a joy caused by good news, success, a blessing.

4. For the believer, deep joy arises from trust in God: "Let us be glad, and rejoice in His salvation!" (Isaiah 25:9). It is a spiritual joy, rooted not in oneself but in God and His works.
H8055.origine: The Hebrew verb samach carries the idea of supporting, of making stand. The root expresses the idea that joy "lifts up" the heart. The word comes from the same family as "sam'ach" (support). It is a fundamental word in the emotional vocabulary of the Old Testament, very frequent especially in the Psalms and the books of celebration.
H8055.emploi: This verb appears 147 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is abundant in the Psalms (over 30 occurrences), the historical books, and particularly in accounts of religious festivals. It is found in very varied contexts: personal and intimate joy (Exodus 4:14), collective and festive joy (Deuteronomy 12:7), religious joy in the presence of God (Psalms 32:11, 96:11), but also carnal or ambiguous joy (Proverbs 15:30 for visual pleasures). The Lord Himself "rejoices" in His people. The verb can also describe a triumphant joy, almost ironic in the face of enemies (Psalms 35:15, 35:19).
H8055.portee: This word reminds us that joy is a biblical gift, not a guilt. It is not light or futile: it arises from salvation, from trust in God, from His support. For the Christian, learning to rejoice "in the Lord" rather than in oneself is to place their satisfaction and stability in the true foundation. It is to accept that God wants us to be happy, not sad.

sens: Filled with joy, showing cheerfulness
Bringing joy, causing satisfaction
Rejoicing, taking pleasure in something
H8056.detail:
1. The word describes a person or moment filled with visible joy and cheerfulness. It is the state of one who is content, happy, and expresses satisfaction. In Proverbs 15:13, "a joyful heart makes a cheerful face": the joy of the heart is reflected on the face. In 2 Chronicles 7:10, the people made "joyful" by the Lord's blessings are sent back to their tents with this inner gladness.
2. The word can also qualify an activity, moment, or state that brings joy and satisfaction. In Deuteronomy 16:15, the Lord asks His people to engage "fully in joy" during the feast: it is about fully experiencing happiness, rejoicing without reservation. In 1 Kings 4:20, Judah and Israel "were joyful" while eating and drinking: joy accompanies moments of prosperity and abundance.
3. The word can also describe one who rejoices in something, who takes pleasure in it or derives satisfaction from it. In Proverbs 2:14, the wicked rejoice in doing evil: they find pleasure in what is wrong. In Esther 5:14, Haman must go "joyfully" to the feast: he believes he has reasons to rejoice.
H8056.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses contentment, cheerfulness, and satisfaction. It evokes the idea of shining, radiating — the joyful person "shines" from within, their gladness radiates. The word belongs to a family of terms that describe the emotional state and visible expression of joy throughout the body. In the Old Testament, it often denotes the emotion accompanying feasts, banquets, and moments of divine blessing.
H8056.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms, Proverbs, and historical accounts. It describes the state of joy of the people during religious festivals (Deuteronomy 16:15), the prosperity that makes one joyful (1 Kings 4:20), or the joy that comes from God's blessing (2 Chronicles 7:10). It is also encountered to describe the joy of the heart (Proverbs 15:13), or conversely, a false joy, one derived from reprehensible things (Proverbs 2:14 with the wicked, Esther 5:14 with Haman who believes he is triumphing before his downfall). Joy can be righteous (linked to God and His blessings) or misguided (based on pride or evil).
H8056.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the true source of joy: it comes from God, from His blessings and His love. It is not a luxury, but a natural response to divine grace. At the same time, the Bible shows that joy can be misguided when sought in evil or pride: the true joy of the heart is that which radiates from one who lives according to God. For the Christian, it is a call to rejoice without fear in the Lord, knowing that this lasting gladness comes from Him alone.

sens: State of cheerfulness, contentment, pleasure felt
Gladness expressed through feasts, songs, celebrations
Joy arising from a happy event, from deliverance
Joy that God provides to those who seek Him
State of satisfaction or inner well-being
Joy as a fruit of a righteous heart
H8057.detail:
1. Joy is primarily a feeling of contentment and pleasure. It is the happy state of one whose heart is at peace. In the Psalms, it is said that "light is sown for the righteous, and joy for those whose hearts are upright": those who live in righteousness experience this inner joy.

2. Joy is also expressed through noisy and joyful celebrations: songs, tambourines, shared meals. When Laban reproaches Jacob for fleeing without saying goodbye, he says: "I would have let you go amid rejoicing and songs, with the sound of tambourine and harp." Joy is here what is seen and heard.

3. Joy arises from good news, from deliverance. In the book of Esther, when the king's decree saves the Jews from massacre, "wherever the king's order and edict arrived, there was joy and gladness among the Jews, feasting and celebrations." It is the joy of one who escapes misfortune.

4. Joy can also be that which God gives. It crowns the heart of one who seeks Him. It is a gift from God to the righteous, as when the Psalms announce: "everlasting joy shall crown their heads" for the redeemed of the Lord.

5. Joy is a state of satisfaction in the good things and happy moments of life. Ecclesiastes explores this feeling: "what is the use of joy?" he wonders, but also: "I gave myself to joy" with pleasures and feasts.

6. Finally, joy belongs to one whose heart is upright before God. It is an inner fruit of righteousness, a blessing attached to a just walk.
H8057.origine: The word simchah comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of rejoicing and cheerfulness. It is a noun that designates both the inner state (the feeling) and its external expression (the feast, the songs). In Hebrew, this word is closely related to the idea of a happy life and complete satisfaction. Joy in the Bible is never limited to a mere private feeling: it is always publicly expressed, through celebrations and sharing.
H8057.emploi: The word simchah appears 89 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms (over 25 occurrences), Chronicles (15 times), Ecclesiastes (9 times), and Isaiah (8 times). It is also found in historical accounts (1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings) and in the wisdom books. Joy appears as a divine blessing for the righteous (Psalms 97:11), a feeling that accompanies victories and deliverances (Esther, Ezra), but also a theme that wisdom interrogates (Ecclesiastes). It arises in solemn moments: dances before the ark (2 Samuel 6:12), temple feasts (2 Chronicles 29:30), restoration after the return from exile (Ezra 3:12-13). Joy can also be withdrawn as punishment (Jeremiah 7:34), which shows its character as a divine blessing.
H8057.portee: Joy is a gift from God for the upright heart, not a mere hedonistic pleasure. It accompanies the walk in righteousness and faith. Discovering this word invites the Christian to distinguish true joy, which comes from God and the feeling of His presence, from false pleasures that do not satisfy. It is also to understand that biblical joy is not afraid to express itself publicly, through celebration, song, and sharing.

sens: To let fall, to drop
To lean down, to sag under weight
To abandon a burden, a debt, a right
To allow to rest, to grant a pause
H8058.detail:
1. To let fall or drop something: this is the most physical and concrete meaning of the word. When Uzzah reached out to steady the ark of God, the oxen carrying it caused it to lean (2 Samuel 6:6), meaning it sagged under its own weight.
2. To lean or incline downward: the word describes the movement of a load that gives way, that tips over. The ark "leaned" on the oxen because the weight made them bend (1 Chronicles 13:9).
