3. To release in the sense of renouncing a right or a claim: this is the figurative, moral, and legal sense. In the seventh year, creditors were to release the debts of their Israelite brothers, meaning to renounce them without claiming them (Deuteronomy 15:2-3). The word moves from the physical (to let fall) to the social (to let go of a claim).
4. To grant rest or relaxation: the seventh year was called a "release" for the land — cultivation ceased to allow it to rest (Exodus 23:11). It is a moment of cessation of work.
H8058.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁמַט (shamat) comes from a root that denotes the action of letting go, of relinquishing. The basic image is that of a hand opening and letting fall what it held. This same root has given rise to words related to relaxation, rest, and voluntary abandonment. The word belongs to the legal and religious vocabulary of Israel, particularly in the laws of Exodus and Deuteronomy regarding the rest of the land and the remission of debts.
H8058.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the laws of sabbatical rest and jubilee. In Exodus 23:11 and Deuteronomy 15:2-3, it describes the "release" — a legal institution where creditors renounce collecting the debts of their brothers. In parallel, the land itself was to be "released" (left to rest) every seven years. In 2 Samuel 6:6 and 1 Chronicles 13:9, the word describes the ark that "leans" under the weight of the oxen. In 2 Kings 9:33, it means to throw someone down — to let a person fall from the top of a wall. The word thus navigates between the physical idea of letting fall and the legal or liturgical idea of renouncing and ceasing.
H8058.portee: This word reminds us that in God's plan for Israel, freedom and rest held a central place. The release of debts was not a one-time act of charity, but a legal obligation that regularly redefined social relations: no one could remain forever crushed by debt. Similarly, the rest of the land every seven years taught that productivity was not an absolute, and that God alone ensured sustenance. For the Christian, this word evokes the idea of liberation: Christ accomplished this definitive "release" by erasing our debt of sin through his death and resurrection.

sens: Year every seven years when debts are canceled
Remission or cancellation of a debt
Cessation of work and the right to pursue a claim
H8059.detail: 1. The release is a holy year that occurs every seven years in the calendar of Israel. It is an institution of Mosaic law intended to relieve the poor and maintain social equality among God's people (Deuteronomy 15:1). 2. Specifically, during this year, every Israelite creditor must renounce his right to pursue in court anyone who owes him money: he releases the debtor from his obligation (Deuteronomy 15:2, where it is said that the creditor "will release his right"). 3. It is also a year of rest: the work of the land ceases, and relationships of domination or constraint are suspended. This release is closely linked to the Feast of Tabernacles and proclaimed in honor of the Lord (Deuteronomy 31:10).
H8059.origine: The Hebrew word shemittah comes from the root shutt, which means "to let go," "to drop," "to release." This image of "letting fall" well expresses the character of the institution: claims are let go, debtors are released. It is a term specific to Mosaic law, embodying the principle of grace and forgiveness every seven years.
H8059.emploi: The word appears four times in Deuteronomy, always to designate the year of release prescribed by the Law. Moses first explains the principle: "you shall release" every seven years (Deuteronomy 15:1). He then details its application: each creditor must refrain from pressuring the debtor and release him from his debt (Deuteronomy 15:2). The emphasis is also on the moral aspect: demanding payment as the release approaches would be a lack of pity toward the poor, which would attract divine judgment (Deuteronomy 15:9). Finally, the year of release was publicly proclaimed at the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 31:10), signaling to all Israel the beginning of this period of grace.
H8059.portee: This institution reveals the merciful heart of the Law of Moses, often misunderstood. It shows that God did not want his children to be crushed by perpetual debt, but to know regular freedom. For the Christian, the release is an image of forgiveness and remission of sins in Jesus Christ: just as Israel was freed from its debts every seven years, the believer is freed from his debt to God by grace.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Onam and descendant of Jerahmeel
Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Rekem, father of Maon and descendant of Caleb
H8060G.detail:
1. Shammai is a descendant of Jerahmeel, son of Onam and brother of Jada. He is the father of Nadab and Abishur, as shown in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2:28. His name means "desolate" or "devastated."
2. Another Shammai appears in the same genealogy, son of Rekem, father of Maon, and from the lineage of Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:44-45). The Bible distinguishes these two men with the same name across different generations.
H8060G.origine: The name Shammai comes from a Hebrew root that means "desolation" or "devastation." Several men bore this name in ancient Israel, particularly in the lines of Judah. It is a characteristic family name of the Israelite people during the time of the divided monarchy.
H8060G.emploi: Shammai is mentioned only in 1 Chronicles, in the detailed genealogy of the sons of Judah. The text first presents him as the son of Onam and brother of Jada (1 Chronicles 2:28), then lists his sons Nadab and Abishur. These genealogies aimed to preserve the memory of the families of Judah after the exile, tracing lineages over several generations. Several individuals named Shammai appear in these lists, indicating that it was a name held by several men of the tribe.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H8060H.detail: Shammai is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb. He appears twice in the text of 1 Chronicles 2, first as the son of Rekem (1 Chronicles 2:44), then as the father of Maon (1 Chronicles 2:45). He is part of the long genealogical chain of God's people, illustrating how the tribes of Israel preserved the memory of their lineages during the division of the kingdom between Israel and Judah.
H8060H.origine: The name Shammai literally means "desolate" or "desolation" in Hebrew. Its etymology refers to the idea of devastation or ruin, although the meaning of the name remained largely symbolic among the Israelites who bore it.
H8060H.emploi: Shammai is mentioned twice in the Bible, only in the context of the genealogies of Judah reported in the second chapter of 1 Chronicles. He appears in the complex family tree of the tribe of Judah and the house of Caleb, establishing the familial links that organized the clan structure of Israel. These mentions are part of the genealogical records that structured the identity of the people and the distribution of land after the return from exile.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Israel before the monarchy
H8060I.detail: Schammaï is a man of Judah, son of Mered and Bithiah, brother of Miriam and Ishbah (1 Chronicles 4:17). He appears in the genealogical lists of the tribe of Judah, particularly in the lineage of Jerahmeel. His name means "desolate" or "abandoned" in Hebrew, although his role in the history of Israel remains limited to this simple genealogical mention.
H8060I.origine: The name Schammaï comes from a Hebrew root that evokes desolation or abandonment. This name belongs to the family of descriptive Hebrew names that reflect a situation or characteristic. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, each belonging to different lineages of Judah.
H8060I.emploi: Schammaï appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:17, where he is presented as the son of Mered and Bithiah. He is listed in the detailed genealogies of the tribe of Judah, among the descendants of Jerahmeel and Caleb. This genealogical passage enumerates the children of Ezra and his descendants, thus recording Schammaï in the official register of important families of Israel.

sens: son of Gilead and grandson of Manasseh
eponymous ancestor of a family from the tribe of Manasseh
H8061.detail:
1. Schemida is a man from the time of the Exodus and the wilderness, son of Gilead and grandson of Manasseh. He belongs to the genealogy of the tribes of Israel and has several brothers: Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, and Hepher (1 Chronicles 7:19).
2. Schemida became the ancestor of an entire family, the Schemidaites, who received a portion of the territory of Manasseh during the land distribution in Canaan. His sons Achjan, Shechem, Likchi, and Aniam form the foundation of this lineage (Numbers 26:32; Joshua 17:2).
H8061.origine: The name Schemida means "wise" or "one who knows" in Hebrew. It is formed from a root that refers to knowledge and wisdom. The patronymic "Schemidaites" designates the descendants who bear his name, a common practice in Israel to identify family clans.
H8061.emploi: Schemida is mentioned three times in the Bible, each time in a genealogical context. First in Numbers 26:32, during the census of the Israelites in the wilderness, where his family is listed among those of Manasseh. Then in Joshua 17:2, when the lands are distributed to the sons of Manasseh according to their families—the Schemidaites receive their inheritance there. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 7:19, a detailed genealogy enumerates his four sons. These three passages highlight the administrative and genealogical importance of Schemida in the tribe of Manasseh.

sens: descendant of Shemida
member of the Shemida clan
H8062.detail:
1. A Schemidaïte is a descendant of Shemida, son of Gilead and grandson of Manasseh. Shemida was a man of the tribe of Manasseh during the time of Egypt and the wilderness.
2. In practice, this term designates the members of the clan or family who bore the name of Shemida. During the census in Numbers 26, the Israelite families are enumerated by their ancestors: the Schemidaites thus form a unit of the tribe of Manasseh, alongside other families like the Hepherites.
H8062.origine: The word "Schemidaïte" comes from the proper name Shemida. According to some, the name Shemida would mean "wise" or could evoke knowledge (a root related to the idea of knowing). The suffix "-aïte" in French (or "-ite" in Hebrew and Greek) is that of clan or tribe names, as found for the Reubenites, Gadites, Benjaminites—it indicates belonging to a family group descended from an ancestor.
H8062.emploi: The term "Schemidaïte" appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:32, during the second census of the people of Israel in the plains of Moab. This passage enumerates the families of the tribe of Manasseh and names them by their ancestors. Shemida is presented as a son of Gilead, himself a son of Manasseh, which anchors this clan in the genealogy of the twelve tribes.
H8062.portee: This passage reminds us that each believer belongs to a genealogy, a history, and a people chosen by God. The census emphasizes God's faithfulness, who counts and knows each of His children by name and by their lineage.

sens: piece of fabric or thick material intended to cover and protect
thick fabric thrown over someone to hide or warm them
H8063.detail:
1. A covering is a piece of fabric or thick material, often of fine quality, that is thrown over a bed, a piece of furniture, or a person to protect them from the cold or to cover them. In Judges 4:18, Jael hides Sisera under a covering in her tent: this is a practical and discreet use of a thick piece of fabric.
2. By extension, this word also designates a garment or fabric capable of concealing, covering, or protecting someone. The image is that of a protective or hidden envelope.
H8063.origine: The Hebrew word שְׂמִיכָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of covering or throwing over someone. It is a feminine noun formed on this basis, which literally designates what covers and envelops. The word belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of textiles and household items in the biblical world.
H8063.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 4:18. It describes the moment when Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, welcomes the Canaanite general Sisera who is fleeing after his defeat. She offers him to rest under her tent and hides him under a thick covering. Shortly thereafter, while he sleeps, she kills him by driving a tent peg through his temple. This detail of the covering underscores both the welcoming and deceptive nature of Jael's hospitality: she offers the fugitive apparent protection that becomes the setting for his condemnation.
H8063.portee: This word reminds us how the Bible cares about concrete human details: clothing, shelters, everyday gestures. In this dramatic passage, the covering highlights the irony of the scene: the one who believes he finds refuge and safety finds death there. It is an invitation to recognize that only the Lord offers true protection.

sens: The visible space above the earth, where clouds, the atmosphere, and air are found
The apparent vault where stars shine and where the sun and moon move
The extent of the visible universe, the entirety of the material creation above us
The dwelling place of God, the seat of His authority and power
The kingdom of God, His spiritual and eternal domain
H8064.detail:
1. Heaven primarily refers to the observable space above our heads: the clouds, the air, everything that floats or flies. In Genesis 1:20, "the birds of the heaven" clearly shows this everyday physical reality. It is the atmosphere we breathe and see.
2. Heaven is also the starry vault, the realm of the celestial bodies. When God says to Abraham, "Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them" (Genesis 15:5), He is speaking of this sparkling immensity from which light and seasons come. The stars, the moon, and the sun inhabit heaven.
3. Heaven represents the entire universe in its visible and celestial dimension: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1) contrasts heaven with dry land, encompassing all that exists. It is the totality of organized creation.
4. Heaven is the throne of God, His heavenly dwelling. In Psalms 115:3, "Our God is in the heavens; He does all that He pleases" affirms that God reigns from above, invisible but omnipresent. Heaven becomes the place from which God governs and judges.
5. Heaven also symbolizes the kingdom and spiritual authority of God, His eternal domain separate from the earthly world. It is less a physical place than a spiritual reality: the realm where God exercises His absolute sovereignty.
H8064.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) likely comes from an ancient root meaning "high" or "elevated." Its dual form (the grammatical form with two) perhaps suggests the idea of "two heights" or "two spheres" — an ancient understanding of heaven as a double expanse. The word first designates the observable reality, before gradually taking on a theological weight: heaven becomes the symbol of God's transcendence and power, His invisible royal seat above the human world.
H8064.emploi: The word "heaven" appears about 395 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis, Psalms, and the prophets. At the beginning of Genesis, it describes the created order: God separates the waters from heaven from those of the earth (Genesis 1:6-8), places the luminaries there (Genesis 1:14-17), and the birds (Genesis 1:20). In Psalms and Job, heaven illustrates the greatness and power of God: "Is not God high in the heavens?" (Job 22:12). The prophets use it to describe divine interventions: fire from heaven (Genesis 19:24), rain (Deuteronomy 11:17), or calamities sent by God (Deuteronomy 28:23-24). Heaven progressively embodies transcendence: the inaccessible realm where God dwells, from which He observes and acts upon the earthly world.
H8064.portee: The word "heaven" reminds the biblical reader that God is not limited to the visible and earthly world, but reigns from an infinite height. This establishes a profound relationship between the temporal and the eternal, the human and the divine: what we see above invites contemplation of the One who dwells beyond the visible. For the believer, heaven becomes a source of hope: the place where God exercises His justice, where He guides history, and toward which His people can lift their eyes with confidence and prayer.

sens: The visible space above the earth, where celestial bodies and birds move
The atmosphere that hovers over the earth and from which rain comes
The dwelling place of God and the divine world, the seat of His power and secrets
H8065.detail:
1. Heaven primarily refers to the space we see above our heads: where birds fly and stars shine. In Daniel 4:12, it is said that "the birds of the heaven made their nests in its branches," indicating that we are speaking of the physical and visible space.
2. Heaven is also the source of rain and meteorological phenomena. In Daniel 4:33, Nebuchadnezzar "was drenched with the dew of heaven," indicating that heaven sends water from above to the earth.
3. More spiritually, heaven is the place where God dwells and where His secrets are hidden from men. Daniel 2:28 states: "there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets," showing that God inhabits heaven and that it is from there that He makes His will known. Similarly, in Ezra 5:11, speaking of the "God of heaven" means the God who reigns above all, who dominates the entire universe.
H8065.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁמַיִן (shamayim) comes from a root meaning "height" and "elevation." Its etymology remains debated, but the image is clear: what is "up there," the highest place par excellence. The word appears in Hebrew always in the plural (the heavens), perhaps suggesting the idea of multiple expanses or infinite dimension. In the Greek Old Testament, this word generally translates the same Hebrew term that designates both the physical heaven and heaven as the divine dwelling.
H8065.emploi: The word appears 35 times in the provided corpus, almost entirely in the books of Ezra and Daniel, particularly in chapters 4 and 5 of Daniel. In Ezra, it characterizes God as "the God of heaven" (Ezra 5:11; 7:21), an expression that emphasizes His absolute sovereignty. In Daniel, especially in chapters 2 to 7, the word constantly returns to speak of the secrets that God reveals (Daniel 2:28), of the dominion that rises to the heavens (Daniel 4:22), or of the dew of heaven that falls on the earth (Daniel 4:33). The context changes little: heaven remains the place of divine power and hidden knowledge, the realm from which God governs the world.
H8065.portee: For the believing reader, this word reminds us that God does not dwell on earth like us, but in a holy and hidden place, the seat of His infinite wisdom. Understanding that God is "the God of heaven" invites recognition of His sovereign authority over all things, visible and invisible, and to expect from Him alone the revelation of what surpasses us. It is an invitation to humility and trust: what we do not understand on earth, God knows and masters from heaven.

sens: The ordinal number that comes after the seventh and before the ninth in a series
The day that follows seven other days, marking a limit or a liturgical turning point
A moment of renewal or consecration after a completed period
H8066.detail:
1. Eighth simply designates the ordinal number 8 in rank position: after seven comes the eighth. It is the numerical order used to count days, months, or people in a list (for example, the eighth day of the month, or the eighth priest of a class: 1 Chronicles 25:15).

2. In biblical sacrificial and ritual practice, the eighth day holds spiritual significance: it concludes a period of seven days and marks the moment when a sacred action can take place. After the people have celebrated seven days of festivity or a person has waited seven days of purification, the eighth day is often the day of the final offering or consecration (Leviticus 14:23: on the eighth day, the healed leper brings his offering to the priest; Exodus 22:30: on the eighth day, the firstborn must be presented to the Lord).

3. This number also carries symbolic weight: after the seven days of creation and rest, the eighth day begins a new cycle, often associated with resurrection and renewal (Leviticus 23:36: the eighth day concludes the Feast of Tabernacles with a holy convocation).
H8066.origine: Sheminî comes from the root shmn which designates the number eight. It is a classic ordinal number, formed like all Hebrew ordinals. The number eight itself carries in Scripture a symbolic coloring of renewal and resurrection, distinct from the seven days of the created cycle.
H8066.emploi: The word appears 27 times in the Old Testament, almost always in ritual or chronological contexts. It is very frequent in Leviticus (purification of lepers, offering sacrifices, periods of consecration), in Numbers (offerings of the princes during the dedication of the Tabernacle), and in Kings and Chronicles (dedication of the Temple, feasts, organization of the priests). In almost all cases, the eighth day marks the end of a seven-day wait and the beginning of a new action: presentation of the firstborn, final offering after purification, solemn conclusion of a feast. It is a purely technical and narrative word, without variation of meaning.
H8066.portee: For the Christian, the eighth day in the Bible points to renewal and new life. This repetition shows that God structures liturgical time according to cycles of seven days followed by a consecration or renewal: this teaches the importance of waiting, purification, and dedication in the life of faith. Understanding this motif helps to grasp how the Bible prepares and fulfills its promises through regular and significant steps.

sens: stringed musical instrument, probably equipped with eight strings
musical notation or indication of key for singing
H8067.detail:
1. It is a stringed musical instrument that the Levites played to accompany the songs in the temple. The name suggests an instrument with eight strings, distinct from other harps. In 1 Chronicles 15:21, the musicians Matthithia, Eliphelet, and others played "harps with eight strings" to lead the singing during a solemn procession.
2. The word can also refer to a musical indication or a particular key for the interpretation of the psalms: the titles of Psalms 6 and 12 mention "on the harp with eight strings," which likely guides the choir leader on how to interpret these psalms. This resembles our modern indications of key or tempo.
H8067.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "eight." It is formed as a feminine adjective that describes a harp (a feminine instrument in Hebrew). The image is simple: a harp that has eight strings, distinguished from others by this particular number. This number eight could have special significance in the temple music.
H8067.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice as musical notation in the titles of Psalms 6:1 and 12:1, where it indicates how to play these psalms. Once in 1 Chronicles 15:21, where it concretely designates the instrument that certain Levite musicians played. In all cases, it is in the context of sacred music for the service of the temple and praise.
H8067.portee: This word reminds us that the praise of God in the Old Testament was highly organized and musical. The specific instruments, trained musicians, and special notations show the importance given to singing and playing with art and intention before the Lord. This invites the modern believer to consider how they bring their praise with thoughtfulness and excellence.

sens: Spiny plant with sharp points
Bush or area overgrown with brambles and thorns
Hard and sharp substance like stone or diamond
Figuratively: obstacle, difficulty, or destruction
H8068.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a plant or shrub covered with thorns: the brambles and thorns that grow naturally in abandoned fields or uncultivated land (Isaiah 5:6, 7:23-25). It is what grows when the vine is no longer tended: an image of desolation.
2. By extension, it describes land completely covered with this wild and impenetrable vegetation, soil that has become unusable and hostile (Isaiah 32:13). Plowing and cultivation are no longer possible.
3. The word also designates a hard, sharp, and indestructible material: diamond or a precious stone of extreme hardness, capable of engraving diamond (Jeremiah 17:1) or remaining firm in the face of obstacles (Ezekiel 3:9). This is the sense of "diamond" when the Segond translates it thus.
4. Figuratively, the thorn becomes a symbol of what wounds, hinders, or destroys: God's judgment that consumes the thorns and brambles of evil like fire (Isaiah 9:17, 10:17).
H8068.origine: The Hebrew word shamir primarily designates the thorny plant that grows in the arid lands of the Near East. By analogy with the sharp point, it has taken on the meaning of hard and sharp material (stone, diamond). The underlying image is one of sharpness, of what pricks and wounds: a point that penetrates, that does not yield. It is a specifically Hebrew word, without a clear parallel in other Semitic languages.
H8068.emploi: The word appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Zechariah). In Isaiah, it describes the state of desolation of an abandoned land: the vines are no longer cultivated, the brambles and thorns invade the barren soil (Isaiah 5:6; 7:23-25; 32:13). The prophet uses it as an image of judgment: God makes thorns grow where order and fertility once reigned. In passages of judgment and purification (Isaiah 9:17; 10:17), the thorn is what the divine fire consumes and destroys. In Jeremiah and Ezekiel, the word takes on a harder dimension: it symbolizes what engraves or resists, an indestructible material.
H8068.portee: The thorn speaks to the believer of judgment and retribution: when one abandons God's vineyard, when one neglects His Word, sterility and disorder follow. But it also reminds us that only God is capable of burning and consuming evil, even the hardest and most resistant. For the faithful heart, it is an invitation not to become a barren land overrun with thorns: to cultivate the Word, to maintain communion with God.

sens: fortified city in the mountainous district of Judah
H8069G.detail: Shamir is a small city located in the mountainous region of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. It appears in the list of cities that the tribe of Judah received as an inheritance during the division of the promised land (Joshua 15:48). Its exact location in the mountains of Judah is not specified, but it was significant enough to be listed among the localities assigned to the Judeans.
H8069G.origine: The name Shamir literally means "a point" or "a thorn" in Hebrew, perhaps referring to the pointed shape of the mountainous terrain where the city was built, or to its defensive nature.
H8069G.emploi: Shamir appears only once in the biblical text of the Segond, in Joshua 15:48. It is cited in the succession of cities in the mountainous district assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory after the conquest of Canaan. This unique mention would make it a small urban center of lesser importance compared to the larger cities of Judah.

sens: City in the hill country of Ephraim, in Canaan
H8069H.detail: 1. Schamir is a small town located in the mountainous region of Ephraim, in central Canaan. It is the place where the judge Tola lived, who governed Israel for twenty-three years after Abimelech (Judges 10:1-2).
H8069H.origine: The Hebrew name שָׁמִיר (shamir) literally means "thorn" or "point" — an image perhaps evoking the sharpness of the terrain or the harsh nature of the site. This name aligns with the mountainous character of the region where the town was established.
H8069H.emploi: Schamir appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 10 of the book of Judges. It is mentioned as the residence and burial place of the judge Tola, who succeeded Abimelech and ensured a period of relative peace in Israel. The town is located in the hill country of Ephraim, a key region of Israel during the time of the judges.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi
Son of Micah
H8069I.detail:
1. Schamir is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King David organizes the temple service. He appears in the list of descendants of Uzziel, as the son of Micah (1 Chronicles 24:24).
2. His precise role in the worship is not detailed: he is simply recorded among the Levites assigned to priestly functions.
H8069I.origine: The name Schamir means "a thorn" or "a point" in Hebrew. It is a name that evokes something sharp or piercing. The same name has been borne by other people and places in the Old Testament, but here it designates this particular Levite.
H8069I.emploi: Schamir appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 24:24, during the counting of the Levites under David. He is presented as the son of Micah and grandson of Uzziel, placing him in the genealogy of the temple servants. No additional details about his life or actions are provided by the Bible.

sens: Levite musician in the service of King David
Levite during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah
H8070G.detail:
1. Schemiramoth is a Levite from the family of Merari, meaning a descendant of Levi through the Merari branch. He appears in David's team of musicians who celebrate the arrival of the ark of the covenant in Jerusalem. He plays the harp (or lyre) and is part of the second rank of singers, alongside Zechariah, Jehiel, Mattithiah, and others (1 Chronicles 15:18, 20 and 16:5).
2. A Levite bearing the same name also served during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, according to biblical tradition, although the details of his service are not specified in the provided contexts.
H8070G.origine: The name literally means "name of the heights" (in Hebrew: "shem" = name, "rama" = height). It is a typical compound name of the time, reflecting either a personal characteristic or a connection to a place. Three characters bear this name in the Bible, all related to temple or worship service.
H8070G.emploi: Schemiramoth appears three times in the chronicles of David, always in the context of the musical service of the Temple. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 15:18 and 15:20 during the installation of the ark of the covenant, where he is counted among the Levite musicians playing stringed instruments. He reappears in 1 Chronicles 16:5 in the list of chief musicians established for regular service before the ark. His repeated inclusion suggests an honorable and stable place in the musical hierarchy of the Temple.

sens: Levite during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah
H8070H.detail: Schemiramoth is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King Jehoshaphat of Judah sends religious teachers to the cities of his kingdom to instruct the people in the Law of God. His name appears among a list of Levites and priests charged with this teaching mission (2 Chronicles 17:8). He is one of the thirteen leaders of worship and instruction that the king mobilizes to strengthen the knowledge of God among his people.
H8070H.origine: The name Schemiramoth literally means "name of the heights" or "he who guards the heights": it combines the idea of name (identity) with that of height (elevation, eminence). This man lived during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah, at a time when the Northern and Southern kingdoms had separated.
H8070H.emploi: Schemiramoth appears only once in Scripture, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He is cited as one of the Levites sent by King Jehoshaphat to teach the people. The mention of his name in an official list of religious leaders indicates that he held a position of trust and authority in the temple worship structure. His role was to instruct the inhabitants of the cities of Judah in the knowledge of the Law of the Lord.

sens: Piece of fabric worn on the body for covering
Set of garments and clothing
Particular garment, tunic, or coat
Figuratively: envelope, that which covers something
H8071.detail: 1. Clothing primarily refers to any fabric worn on the body for covering and protection. In Genesis 9:23, Shem and Japheth take a cloak to cover their father Noah's nakedness: this is an act of respect and modesty. 2. The word is also used in the plural for the entirety of garments one possesses, such as the clothes the Hebrews received from the Egyptians when leaving Egypt (Exodus 12:35). 3. In certain contexts, it designates a particular, distinct, or remarkable garment: thus Ruth puts on her best clothes to go find Boaz (Ruth 3:3), or Pharaoh dresses Joseph in a new tunic when bringing him out of prison (Genesis 41:14). 4. Figuratively, clothing also evokes that which covers or envelops: Isaiah 4:1 speaks of a symbolic mantle of blessing, and Psalm 102 compares the heavens to a garment that God can remove (Proverbs 30:4).
H8071.origine: The Hebrew word שִׂמְלָה (simla) comes from a root meaning to wrap or cover. It concretely describes what protects the body from the climate and from prying eyes. The word is used in the singular for a particular garment or coat, and in the plural for the entirety of clothing. It is a very common word in biblical Hebrew, used in the oldest narratives and in legislation.
H8071.emploi: The word simla appears 28 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Judges, Samuel) and among the prophets. Its usage varies according to context: it means a cloak one wears (Genesis 9:23), clothes one possesses (Exodus 12:35), a new garment given as a sign of honor (Genesis 41:14), or clothing that is torn as a sign of mourning or grief (Genesis 37:34, Joshua 7:6). The law in Deuteronomy uses it to speak of identity and the difference between men and women (Deuteronomy 22:5). The word can also simply evoke material possessions, such as when they are offered as gifts or spoils.
H8071.portee: Clothing in the Bible is never a mere material necessity: it expresses honor, identity, and inner state. Dressing someone in fine clothing restores dignity and power (like Joseph), while tearing one's clothes reveals mourning or distress of heart. For the Christian, this word reminds us that God cares about our concrete needs, and that outward appearance often reflects an inner spiritual reality.

sens: King of Moab, successor of Hadad
H8072.detail: Samla is a king of Moab who reigned after the death of Hadad. The Bible mentions him in the genealogical lists of the kings of Edom, where he is presented as originating from Masrekah. He was succeeded by Saul of Rehoboth, as reported in Genesis 36:36-37 and its parallels in 1 Chronicles 1:47-48.
H8072.origine: The name Samla literally means "garment" in Hebrew, although the reason for this royal name is not explained in the biblical texts. He is listed among the kings of Edom, a neighboring region of Israel, whose genealogy interested the biblical writers.
H8072.emploi: Samla appears four times in the Bible: twice in Genesis 36:36-37, in the list of kings of Edom before Israel had a king, and twice in 1 Chronicles 1:47-48, which reproduces the same text. At each mention, he is placed between King Hadad and King Saul, confirming his place in the royal succession of Edom. No particular details are given about his reign or deeds.

sens: Make desolate, empty, uninhabitable — a country, a city, a temple
Completely destroy the property, resources, life of a person
Be seized with horror, dread at the sight of destruction
Cause horror, astonishment by the magnitude of the disaster
H8074G.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the transformation of a fertile region into an arid desert: once-populated cities become silent and empty, roads are no longer frequented. It is the image of a land that no one inhabits anymore. Ezekiel 33:28 states clearly: "the mountains of Israel will be desolate; no one will pass through them."
2. The word also applies to the destruction of personal property: a house is ravaged, livestock is destroyed, crops are plundered. Job 16:7 expresses this devastation: "You have ravaged my entire house."
3. The word can also refer to an emotional state: being horrified, struck with astonishment at the extent of misfortune. It is the dread that seizes one when witnessing ruin.
4. Sometimes the word describes the effect that catastrophe has on the observer: it causes horror, moral desolation. Lamentations 5:18 testifies to this: "the mountain of Zion is desolated."
H8074G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of devastation and silence — what remains of a destroyed place. The related noun שְׁמָמָה (shemmah) designates the ruin itself. This root is rich: it carries the image of a sterile land, emptied of its substance, where the silence of emptiness reigns. The verb can be conjugated in several ways to express nuances: to be devastated (passive), to devastate oneself (active), or to be struck with horror.
H8074G.emploi: This verb appears 53 times in the Old Testament, mainly among the prophets who threaten Israel or other nations with devastation. Leviticus 26 lists the punishments: devastating animals, deserted roads, ravaged land. Jeremiah and Ezekiel use it extensively to describe the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple. The word also appears in Isaiah, where it contrasts with future restoration: the deserted cities will be repopulated (Isaiah 54:3). In Lamentations, the word expresses the desolation of the ruined Temple. The context is almost always that of divine punishment, enemy conquest, or prophetic threat.
H8074G.portee: This word reminds the reader of the seriousness of sin in the eyes of God and the reality of divine judgment. Devastation is not an abstraction: these are empty cities, barren fields, broken lives. But the Bible often places this word alongside promises of restoration (Isaiah 49:8, 61:4): devastation is never the final word. The Christian finds in it a call to repentance and assurance that God, even in judgment, does not permanently destroy His people.

sens: Be struck with astonishment, shock at something unexpected or terrible
Be stunned, momentarily lose one's composure in the face of a shocking reality
Become dismayed, emptied inside by a catastrophe or overwhelming news
Be ravaged, devastated (referring to a place)
H8074H.detail:
1. To be struck with astonishment, shock: it is the sudden emotion of one who sees or learns something unexpected or horrible. In Job 21:5, others are asked to look and be astonished, meaning to recognize that they are witnessing something extraordinary.
2. To be stunned, momentarily lose one's composure: the word describes one who can no longer speak or act, so great is the shock. Isaiah 63:5 shows someone astonished to find no one to help him — it is a shock mixed with perplexity.
3. To become dismayed, emptied inside: when Ezra learns of the people's unfaithfulness, he tears his clothes and sits down in dismay (Ezra 9:3) — it is a deep consternation that overwhelms the entire being.
4. To be ravaged, devastated: a country, a city can be struck with desolation by war or God's judgment. Leviticus 26:32 threatens that the land will be plundered and the enemies who occupy it will be astonished by its ruin (Jeremiah 19:8).
H8074H.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁמם comes from a root that evokes silence, emptiness, the absence of life. It has given rise to several forms: passive (to be dismayed), active (to devastate), and reflexive (to be stunned). The word always expresses a rupture: what was inhabited or alive becomes deserted, what was organized becomes ruin, what was understandable becomes incomprehensible and strikes silence into the observer.
H8074H.emploi: The word appears 29 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah) and historical narratives. It describes two related realities: human astonishment in the face of catastrophe, and the devastation of lands and cities. In divine threats, God devastates (Hiphil) so that those who see the ruin are astonished (Niphal or Qal). This is particularly frequent in announcements of judgment against Babylon (Jeremiah 50:45) or in descriptions of mourning (Ezra 9:3, where Ezra expresses his dismay by tearing his clothes).
H8074H.portee: This word invites us to be aware of two things: first, that God's judgment on sin produces a real and visible desolation, capable of filling with astonishment those who witness it. Secondly, that astonishment itself can be a call to repentance — when one sees ruin, one is forced to recognize that something serious has occurred. The word reminds us that faith does not spare us from the pain of evil and its consequences, but it helps us interpret them in light of God's plan.

sens: Be struck with surprise and inner turmoil
Be left speechless, stunned in the face of something strange or overwhelming
H8075.detail:
1. To be astonished is to be seized by surprise and emotion in the face of something unexpected or overwhelming. The heart stops, the mind is troubled, one remains paralyzed. This is what Daniel feels when King Nebuchadnezzar recounts his terrifying dream: the prophet is so moved that he remains for a moment unable to react (Daniel 4:19).
2. Beyond mere surprise, it is a form of stupor, a state where turmoil renders one mute or confused. The word can describe the shock effect in the face of destruction, a catastrophe, or an unbearable reality.
H8075.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a root (שׁמם) that means "to be destroyed" or "to be dismayed." The form used here (Ithpolel) is a reflexive form that emphasizes the inner state: one who is struck by something devastating remains astonished, as if he himself were destroyed or annihilated from within. It is the Hebrew שָׁמֵם which has the same root with the meaning of "desert" or "devastated."
H8075.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:19. It describes Daniel's state in the face of the king's terrifying dream: the prophet, although accustomed to visions, is momentarily paralyzed by the emotion and turmoil inspired by this dream. It is not ordinary fear, but a form of stupor, astonishment at something grave and enigmatic. The context shows that it is a very human feeling, even in a man of God.
H8075.portee: This word reminds us that it is normal to be troubled and stunned in the face of great trials, enigmas that surpass us, or God's judgments. Daniel, for all his wisdom, feels the weight of it. This speaks to the humility we must maintain in the face of God's mysteries and the seriousness of His ways.

sens: State of a land ravaged, abandoned, empty of inhabitants
Emotional state of one who is broken, overwhelmed, without resources
Ruins, remnants of a destroyed place
H8076.detail: 1. The word primarily describes a land or country reduced to nothing by destruction: razed cities, abandoned fields, everything that constituted human life has disappeared. Jeremiah 12:11 clearly shows this: the entire land becomes a desert because no one takes care of it — this is the consequence of divine anger. 2. It is also the inner state of one who is struck, crushed by misfortune: a heart emptied of all hope, a wounded soul that can no longer rise. When Tamar, violated, remains desolate in the house of Absalom (2 Samuel 13:20), this word designates her intimate despair as much as her social isolation. 3. The word can refer to physical ruins, the remnants of past destruction: the abandoned cities and desolate ruins of Israel (Ezekiel 36:4) are the visible marks of divine judgment.
H8076.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of being empty, lifeless, completely devoid of substance. It is the image of a desert, a barren land where nothing remains — neither population, nor fertility, nor hope. Biblical desolation is never neutral: it results from God's judgment or the misfortune that strikes the righteous.
H8076.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophetic and poetic books (Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel) and once in Daniel. It designates either the state of the territory of Israel ravaged by invasion (Jeremiah 12:11, Ezekiel 36:4), or the psychological and spiritual state of the people or individual overwhelmed (2 Samuel 13:20, Lamentations 1:13, 3:11). In Daniel's prayer (9:17), the sanctuary itself is said to be devastated, which shows that desolation even reaches the sacred heart of faith. The term encompasses both physical destruction and moral ruin.
H8076.portee: Biblical desolation reminds the reader that sin and unfaithfulness have real and visible consequences, but it never has the final word. Ezekiel 36:4 announces that these ruins will be restored; Daniel's prayer (9:17) pleads for God to restore His sanctuary. For the believer, this word invites recognition of the weight of divine judgment, but also to hope in His restoring mercy.

sens: Land or region that has become completely empty and barren, uninhabitable
Ruins of a city or country destroyed
State of ruin and abandonment, absence of life and activity
Complete solitude, extreme isolation
H8077A.detail:
1. The word first designates a land that has become desolate, empty of all human life. When God says to Jerusalem, "I will make you a desert," He speaks of a city that will be so destroyed that no one will live there anymore (Jeremiah 6:8). It is a dead, abandoned land.

2. The word also applies to material ruins: cities destroyed by war or God's judgment that are nothing but rubble (Jeremiah 44:6 speaks of cities of Judah "that are nothing but ruins"). The walls are razed, the houses burned.

3. It more broadly describes the state of a ravaged and impoverished country: when everything is destroyed, when commerce and life cease, when silence reigns where human voices once echoed (Ezekiel 32:15: "the land will be ravaged"). It is total desolation.

4. Figuratively, the word can evoke isolation or emotional abandonment: being alone, forsaken, separated from others, like an island in the middle of water (Ezekiel 35:15: "You will become a solitude").
H8077A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be empty" or "to be desolate." It is from the same family as words expressing astonishment or horror, as desolation provokes shock. In ancient Hebrew, the word always evokes a loss, a ruin that has struck and inspires fear. It is a state resulting from a destructive action, often that of God in judgment.
H8077A.emploi: This word appears 52 times in the Old Testament, especially in the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel, who describe God's judgment on Judah and the nations. It is used for lands ravaged by invasion (Jeremiah 4:27), for destroyed cities (Jeremiah 44:6), for regions struck by God (Ezekiel 32:15, where Egypt becomes a solitude). The word has nuances: sometimes it designates physical and material ruin (rubble, burned cities), sometimes the total absence of life and inhabitants, sometimes the state of a land that has become wild and uninhabitable. It is always a consequence of divine judgment or destruction.
H8077A.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment is not a vague threat: it leads to concrete ruins, to the destruction of what was alive and prosperous. For the believer, it is a call to take seriously the call to repentance, for God can reduce a city, a kingdom, an entire life to nothing. But the prophetic context also shows that this desolation is not definitive: God can restore and rebuild after judgment.

sens: State of what is deserted and empty of inhabitants
Abandonment of a land that becomes barren and inhospitable
Ruins and devastation of a territory
H8077B.detail: 1. The word first designates a place completely empty of inhabitants and life — a desert where no one lives. In Ezekiel 35:7, the prophet announces that the mountain of Seir will become a solitude: it will be so ravaged that no living creature can remain there. 2. It is also the concrete result of destruction: a fertile land can become a barren and desolate solitude, where even travelers hesitate to pass. The word evokes not only the absence of population but the absence of life altogether. 3. In the biblical context, solitude is often a punishment: God empties a territory of its inhabitants to punish it for its sins, reducing it to a state of abandoned ruins.
H8077B.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be empty" or "to be desolate." It belongs to a family of words expressing devastation and abandonment: the related word שְׁמָמָה (shemaméh) has exactly the same meaning. The root evokes the image of a place that has been emptied of its inhabitants and riches, left in a state of ruin.
H8077B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible translated by Segond, in Ezekiel 35:7. The prophet uses it to describe the divine punishment that will strike the mountain of Seir (the territory of Esau, ancestor of the Edomites): it will become a solitude, empty and ravaged. It is a judgment against a people that has committed iniquity and mistreated the sons of Israel. The word expresses both the absence of life and the physical ruin of the territory.
H8077B.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of divine judgment: sin and iniquity do not go unpunished. A land can be rich and inhabited, but if it opposes God and His people, it can become a barren and abandoned solitude. It is an implicit call to fear God and not to follow the path of those who oppose Him, for the consequences are irreversible and terrible.

sens: State of abandonment and ruin of a city or land
Total absence of inhabitants and life
Feeling of overwhelming despair in the face of such emptiness
H8077G.detail: 1. The word designates concretely a ravaged, uninhabited land, given over to nothingness — a city or territory destroyed by war, invasion, or divine judgment. In Isaiah 62:4, Jerusalem, which remained 'desolate' after the exile, receives the promise of never being called that again: the word evokes physical emptiness and forgetfulness. 2. It is also the image of complete silence, the absence of human life: a desolation is not simply damaged; it is devoid of meaning and inhabitants. 3. Figuratively, the word carries an emotional weight of abandonment and misfortune — not just material ruin, but the spiritual experience of loss and divine judgment.
H8077G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of muteness, of astonishment struck by stupor. It belongs to the family of words describing a deathly silence, an annihilation, a void that renders one mute. In Isaiah 62, it qualifies Jerusalem after the ruin: not only ruined, but rendered silent, emptied of its life and past glory.
H8077G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond 1910: in Isaiah 62:4. This passage is a prophetic promise — God announces that Jerusalem will cease to be called 'desolation' (Abandonment) and will receive a new name, synonymous with restoration and divine favor. It is the moment when the destroyed city emerges from its misfortune. The context is one of redemption and renewal after judgment.
H8077G.portee: This word reminds us that desolation is not the final state for the people of God. Jerusalem experienced total abandonment, the absence of help; but God promises to change its name and restore it. For the Christian, this passage invites belief that even in apparent abandonment, God is preparing a restoration and renewal.

sens: Feeling of intense, almost paralyzing fear, in the face of an impending disaster
Anguish and disgust mixed before imminent ruin
H8078.detail: 1. Terror is an extreme fear that seizes one who sees a disaster approaching — here, the famine that will strike Jerusalem. It is not an ordinary fear, but a terror that invades the whole being. In Ezekiel 4:16, the inhabitants will eat 'with anguish' and drink 'with terror': each meal will become an act laden with fear and horror, as they will know that food is lacking and that the end is near. 2. The word also expresses disgust mixed with fear in the face of an abominable situation. In Ezekiel 12:19, this terror accompanies the certainty that the land will be emptied of everything, pillaged by violence: it is not just being afraid, but being horrified by what one sees and what one knows is coming.
H8078.origine: The Hebrew word shimmamon comes from a root expressing the idea of desolation and stupor — being struck by horror to the point of becoming frozen. The word describes the state of one who is left speechless in the face of horror, unable to react as they are seized by dread.
H8078.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the prophet Ezekiel, in oracles of judgment against Jerusalem. In both cases, it is linked to famine and ruin: the horrification accompanies every daily act of eating and drinking. It is the psychological and spiritual state of those who see punishment approaching. The prophet uses this word to show that judgment will not only be physical — hunger — but also moral and emotional: a permanent terror.
H8078.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment is never abstract. The terror it engenders is real, tangible, penetrating even the most ordinary moments of life. For the believer, it invites taking prophetic warnings and the seriousness of sin seriously, but it also reminds us that God's mercy remains open to those who repent.

sens: small reptile that moves quickly on its four legs
animal capable of climbing even on the walls of royal palaces
H8079.detail: 1. The lizard is a small scaly reptile with four legs, that runs quickly on the ground and can climb vertical surfaces. In Proverbs 30:28, the image of the lizard that 'grabs with its hands and is found in the palaces of kings' shows its remarkable ability to sneak everywhere, even into the most prestigious dwellings, despite its small size. 2. The word also evokes the quiet boldness of a fragile creature that does not hesitate to enter wherever it wants: it symbolizes humility coupled with discreet effectiveness, exactly as the text of Proverbs highlights by listing the four small 'wise' things on the earth.
H8079.origine: The Hebrew word שְׂמָמִית (semamit) specifically designates this small reptile. Its exact etymology remains uncertain, but the word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of Palestinian fauna. In biblical Hebrew, it is one of the terms used to designate reptiles that crawl or move quickly.
H8079.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 30:28. It is part of a list of four small creatures that possess remarkable wisdom: the spider that weaves its web, the ant, the lizard, and the locust. The author of the book of Proverbs uses the lizard as an example of practical wisdom — its ability to move skillfully and access the most inaccessible places, including royal palaces, despite its tiny size. It is a wisdom of adaptation and silent effectiveness.
H8079.portee: The lizard teaches us that it is not necessary to be big or powerful to succeed: practical intelligence, agility, and perseverance are worth more than brute strength. This passage invites the reader to value a form of discreet and effective wisdom in daily life, one that finds paths when everything seems blocked.

sens: To become fat or obese, to gain weight
To eat abundantly and be satisfied
Figuratively: to become insensitive, hard-hearted
To prosper materially, to enjoy luxury and ease
H8080.detail:
1. The literal sense is physical: to become fat, to gain weight. In Deuteronomy 32:15, Israel is described as 'grown fat, thick, and sleek', an image of a people that has fattened itself through abundance.
2. To eat excessively and be fully satisfied: in Nehemiah 9:25, the people 'ate, were satisfied, and grew fat' in the fertile lands conquered, tasting material abundance.
3. Figuratively, the heart can 'fatten' or become insensitive: in Isaiah 6:10, God asks to make the people's heart 'insensitive', as if excess made them deaf to God's voice, unable to understand and repent.
4. Fattening also means to prosper and enjoy material ease: in Jeremiah 5:28, the wicked men 'grow fat, shining with obesity' and prosper in evil, forgetting their duties to the poor.
H8080.origine: The Hebrew verb shaman (שָׁמֵן) comes from a root that primarily evokes fat, oil, physical abundance. It thus primarily designates the becoming fat of a body nourished to satisfaction. The image naturally extends figuratively: one who fattens materially ends up becoming morally insensitive, as if wealth numbs the conscience.
H8080.emploi: This verb appears four times in the received texts, always in a moral or theological perspective. In Deuteronomy 32:15 and Nehemiah 9:25, fattening marks the state of prosperity of Israel, which has eaten its fill in fertile lands, but this well-being diverts it from its God. In Isaiah 6:10 and Jeremiah 5:28, the verb shifts to the figurative: the heart fattens to the point of becoming insensitive to the divine word, or the wicked prosper while forgetting justice. The context always emphasizes a spiritual danger: material abundance corrupts.
H8080.portee: This word teaches the believer that material abundance is never spiritually neutral. It can fatten the soul with indifference towards God and injustice towards the poor. The contrast between bodily well-being and the death of the heart calls for vigilance: prosperity demands careful guarding of moral conscience and openness to God's voice.

sens: Liquid fatty substance extracted from olives, used as a staple food
Material used as medicine or ointment for healing or beautifying
Consecrated oil for worship rituals and religious anointings
Substance used to light and maintain the lamps of the sanctuary
Wealth and fertility (poetic image)
H8081.detail:
1. Olive oil is the fundamental agricultural product in the biblical land. It was extracted from olives and used as food: it was poured over bread, used to dip dishes, and cooked with food. This is why the Israelites included it in their offerings at the temple, for example, by pouring oil over flour in certain sacrifices (Leviticus 2:1-7).
2. Oil also served as a remedy and cosmetic. It was applied to wounds, used to anoint the body after bathing, and mixed with perfumes to beautify the skin. Healed lepers received oil poured on their hands as a sign of purification (Leviticus 14:15-18).
3. Consecrated by God, anointing oil was reserved for sacred rituals: it anointed priests upon their inauguration and kings at their coronation. It was a sign of divine election and the outpouring of the Spirit. Aaron received this anointing, symbolizing his priesthood (Numbers 35:25).
4. Oil fueled the lamps of the sanctuary, particularly the sacred lampstand. It burned continually so that the light would never leave the holy place, reminding of God's constant presence (Exodus 27:20).
5. Figuratively, oil symbolizes abundance and prosperity: fertile lands are described as "fat" with oil, an image of rich and well-provided regions. The prophet Isaiah mentions the yoke that breaks under the fatness (Isaiah 10:27), meaning that the wealth brought by divine anointing breaks the chains of oppression.
H8081.origine: The Hebrew word shemet primarily means the fatty substance itself. It comes from an ancient root common to Semitic languages. The olive has been cultivated in the Mediterranean for millennia, and the oil produced from it is one of the most important products of daily and religious life in Israel. The Bible distinguishes between ordinary oil, used for cooking and care, and holy oil, mixed with perfumes for worship rituals.
H8081.emploi: This word appears more than 175 times in the Hebrew Bible, present in almost all historical, legal, and wisdom books. The densest usages are found in Exodus and Leviticus, where the rules of worship at the tabernacle are codified: preparation of anointing oil, composition of holy oil, use for sacrifices and the illumination of the sanctuary. Jacob poured oil on the stone at Bethel to mark his encounter with God (Genesis 28:18). In the Psalms and Proverbs, oil becomes an image of joy, prosperity, and divine blessing. Each context adds a nuance: nourishing oil, therapeutic oil, sacred oil, or symbolic oil of wealth.
H8081.portee: For the Christian, biblical oil is much more than an agricultural product: it symbolizes the active presence of the Holy Spirit, who consecrates, purifies, comforts, and nourishes the soul. The image of anointing oil reminds us that we are anointed by God from the moment of our conversion. The lampstand that burns continually also reminds us of our call to let the light of Christ shine in our lives, fueled by the Holy Spirit. The fertility mentioned in the Bible invites us to embrace the spiritual wealth that God wants to pour out on those who obey Him.

sens: Containing a lot of fatty material, rich in fat
Abundant, fertile, generous in resources
Robust, stocky, well-nourished
Luxurious, sumptuous, offering delights
H8082.detail:
1. Fat primarily means what is rich in fatty material: Asher "produces excellent food" because his lands yield rich and delicate dishes (Genesis 49:20). It is a concrete wealth that nourishes and satisfies.

2. Fat applies to lands and pastures: a fat land is fertile, productive, generous. The spies in Canaan asked if the land was "fat or lean" (Numbers 13:20), as a fat land promises harvests and prosperity. Nehemiah celebrates the "vast and fertile land" that God gave to Israel (Nehemiah 9:35).

3. For people, fat describes one who is well-nourished, robust, vigorous. The Moabite warriors were "robust" and valiant (Judges 3:29), meaning strong and well-muscled due to abundance.

4. Figuratively, fat evokes luxury and abundance: living in delights, enjoying God's blessings. Israel "ate, was satisfied, and grew fat" in prosperity (Nehemiah 9:25), an image of a fulfilled life.
H8082.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses wealth and abundance. It appears in the concrete vocabulary of daily life: food, animals, lands. The concept of fat is inseparable from that of prosperity and material blessing in ancient biblical mentality. A fat pasture is the promise of healthy livestock; rich food is a sign of a generous table.
H8082.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Old Testament. It is used for foods (Genesis 49:20), lands and pastures (Numbers 13:20, Nehemiah 9:25, 9:35), and to describe robust individuals (Judges 3:29). It is also found among the prophets to describe the lands that the Lord grants as a blessing (Ezekiel 34:14, 34:16). Its meaning oscillates between the concrete (rich in fat, fertile) and the figurative (prosperous, abundant). It often carries a positive tone: it is a mark of divine blessing, of life in abundance.
H8082.portee: This word reminds us that God's blessing also manifests in concrete things: fertile land, sufficient food, bodily strength. It invites us to see God's generosity in creation. However, the Bible also shows that Israel forgot its God amid this abundance (Nehemiah 9:25-35), a warning that material prosperity does not guarantee the faithfulness of the heart.

sens: The whole number that comes after seven
The one that occupies the eighth place in an order, a series
Combined with other numbers to form totals
H8083.detail:
1. The word designates the number 8 as a simple and cardinal quantity: it is the digit you count when enumerating objects or people. For example, Adam lived 800 years after the birth of Seth (Genesis 5:4), and Noah's ark rested on the mountains in the seventh month to land on the eighth day (Genesis 8:4).
2. Also used as an ordinal number, "eighth" designates the position or order: the eighth year of a king's reign (2 Chronicles 34:3) is the year that comes after seven other completed years. It is a common chronological marker in royal and historical accounts.
3. The word is frequently used in numerical compositions to form larger totals: "twenty-eight" (1 Chronicles 12:35), "one hundred eighty-eight" (Nehemiah 7:26). It is a simple building block in the construction of complex numbers.
H8083.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the number 8. In Hebrew, the number also has a symbolic dimension: the 8 often represents what transcends the established order of the week (7 days) and marks a new beginning or renewal. This is why circumcisions are performed on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12), symbolizing entry into the covenant. It is a very ancient word, used as early as the first biblical texts.
H8083.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Bible: it appears more than 105 times, especially in historical and genealogical books. It is constantly found in the lists of Genesis (genealogies of the patriarchs: Genesis 5:4, 5:7, 5:10), in the counting of the tribes (Numbers 2:24, 3:28, 4:48), in the architectural descriptions of the temple (1 Kings 7:10: stones of 8 cubits), and in royal chronologies (2 Chronicles 34:3, 2 Kings 22:3). It is used to date reigns, count soldiers, Levites, treasures, and measures. Its use is purely mathematical and informative: the number itself has no variable nuance according to contexts.
H8083.portee: This word does not carry spiritual significance in itself: it is a simple tool to convey precise and verifiable information. It reminds us that the Bible is rooted in real history, with numbers, dates, and lists that place God's people in concrete time and space. For the reader, it is a sign of seriousness and reliability of the biblical narrative.

sens: The number 80, or 8 times 10
The corresponding ordinal: the eightieth
A number used in combination with other numbers
H8084.detail:
1. The number 80 designates a precise quantity: four times twenty. It is a figure that often appears to count people, years, or objects in biblical accounts. Moses was 80 years old when he began his ministry (Exodus 7:7), and Barzillai, an elderly man, described himself as being eighty years old, too old to enjoy life (2 Samuel 19:35).
2. The word can also express the ordinal, that is, the rank: the eightieth day, the eightieth day, etc., although this usage is less common in the provided texts.
3. In composition, the number 80 adds to others to form larger numbers, such as 185 (180 + 5), 186 (180 + 6), or 188 (180 + 8), very frequent for counting warriors or inhabitants (Numbers 2:9: one hundred eighty-six thousand men of Judah).
H8084.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁמֹנִים (shemonîm) comes from the root שְׁמֹנֶה (shemone), which means 8. The number 8 is combined with the suffix of the tens to obtain 80, that is, 8 × 10. It is a simple cardinal number, formed like all multiples of ten in ancient Hebrew.
H8084.emploi: This word appears 37 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in census accounts (Numbers, Chronicles) and genealogies. It designates the age of patriarchs or important figures (Moses, Abraham, Barzillai), the number of soldiers in an army or builders of a temple, or quantities of various objects. The context is generally statistical or narrative: enumerating, counting, establishing a magnitude. Its meaning remains constant from one passage to another: it is always the number 80, whether referring to years, fighters, or priests.

sens: Perceive by the ear a sound, a voice, a word
Learn something, be informed
Pay attention, listen with interest
Accept, consent to a request
Obey an order or instruction
Answer a prayer, respond favorably
H8085G.detail:
1. Hear in the physical sense: perceive sounds by the ear. When Adam and Eve "heard the voice of the Lord God" in the garden of Eden (Genesis 3:8), they literally perceived this voice approaching. This is the simplest and most common meaning.

2. Learn or be informed: receive news, be warned. When Jacob's sons "heard" that Joseph was alive (Genesis 45:16), they discovered it through what was reported to them, not necessarily by listening to him speak directly.

3. Listen attentively, pay attention: "Listen then, house of David!" cries the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 7:13), inviting them to pay attention and welcome the word. Listening here implies interest and receptivity.

4. Consent or accept: agree with someone. When Abraham asks the children of Heth to sell him a tomb and they respond, "we hear you" (Genesis 23:11), they mean that they accept and consent to his request.

5. Obey: submit to an order or instruction. "So that all the people may hear and fear" (Deuteronomy 17:13) means that the people must learn the sentence and submit to it, allowing themselves to be instructed and corrected.

6. Answer: respond favorably to a prayer or supplication. When the Lord says, "I have heard your prayer" (1 Kings 9:3) or when the believer cries out, "I will hear you" (Jeremiah 29:12), it means that the request is heard and there will be a response.
H8085G.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the action of straining the ear, of listening. The Hebrew word שָׁמַע (shamaʿ) is at the heart of biblical spirituality: it does not denote passive listening, but active reception, often linked to submission and obedience. The same root is found in the name שְׁמַע (Shema), the great profession of faith of Israel ("Hear, O Israel"). This richness of the word reflects Hebrew theology: for God, to hear is inseparable from responding, obeying, and allowing oneself to be transformed by what has been heard.
H8085G.emploi: This verb appears about 900 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent words. It is encountered in all contexts: narratives (patriarchs hearing voices or learning news), the Law ("hear the commandments"), prayer ("hear my supplication"), and prophecy ("hear the word of the Lord"). The meaning subtly evolves: "hearing" a voice is primarily a physical action (Genesis 3:8), but "hearing" a request implies acceptance (Genesis 23:11), and "hearing" the Lord engages the whole person in obedience and faith. The texts show that in the Bible, truly hearing means receiving the word in a way that allows one's life to be transformed.
H8085G.portee: For the Christian, this word invites an authentic listening to God. Hearing is not a passive or distracted act: it is positioning oneself to receive, understand, and above all, obey. The Bible calls the believer to "hear" the voice of the Lord not only with their ears but with all their heart, knowing that this listening engages their commitment to God. It is also a promise: God Himself hears the prayers and cries of His people, and He answers those who sincerely seek Him.

sens: Perceive a sound with the ear
Listen to someone attentively
Understand what is said
Accept and follow an order or advice
Submit to someone's authority
Consent to a request
H8085H.detail:
1. Perceiving a sound: the simplest and most literal meaning of the verb. It is primarily the physical act of hearing a noise, a voice, or a word.
2. Listening attentively: this means actively lending an ear, turning one's attention to what is being said. The psalmist describes enemies who "submit to the mere sound of our fame" (Psalm 18:45), which evokes the attention given to a voice.
3. Understanding a language: grasping the meaning of what is heard. Abraham "listened to" his wife's voice (Genesis 27:8) — he did not merely hear sounds, he understood her words and what she was asking.
4. Accepting and following an order: this is the heart of the verb. To obey is to receive a command and put it into practice. Deuteronomy repeatedly emphasizes this idea: "If you obey the commandments" (Deuteronomy 11:27), it means accepting to do what is prescribed.
5. Submitting to authority: recognizing that one is not free to do as one wishes, but must submit to an authority. Abraham "obeyed my voice" means he placed himself under God's authority (Genesis 22:18).
6. Consenting to a request: Rebekah urges Jacob: "My son, obey my voice" (Genesis 27:13) — accepting what she asks with a willing heart.
H8085H.origine: The word comes from a very ancient Hebrew root that primarily means "to hear" — hence its connection to the ear. However, in biblical Hebrew, "to hear" inherently includes the idea of truly listening, that is, receiving and accepting what is heard. The root is found in words of the same family: "oïe" (the ear), "oyant" (the one who listens). This shift in meaning — from "perceiving a sound" to "accepting an order" — reflects Semitic thought: one can truly "hear" a word from God or a command only if it is received in the heart and put into practice.
H8085H.emploi: The verb "obey" appears 122 times in the Hebrew Bible, first in the narratives of the patriarchs. Abraham "obeyed" God by leaving his country and being willing to sacrifice his son (Genesis 22:18). However, the word is particularly frequent in Deuteronomy, which poses the central question: Will Israel keep the covenant by obeying the law of the Lord, or will it refuse to listen? (Deuteronomy 11:27-28). The prophets use it to accuse Israel of having "refused to listen" to calls for repentance (Nehemiah 9:29, Jeremiah 25:8). The word encompasses the entire range: from the simple act of listening to a voice to the voluntary decision to submit to God. What unites all these uses is the idea that truly receiving a word means obeying it.
H8085H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word raises the eternal question: how do I relate to the word of God? Do I "listen" to God only with the edge of my ears, or do I "obey," meaning I receive His word in my heart and put it into practice? The Bible says that blessing comes to those who listen and obey (Deuteronomy 28:1-2). But it also highlights the weight of refusal: Israel refused to listen, and the consequences were severe. It is a call to take the Word seriously — not just to read it, but to receive it and live it out.

sens: Perceive a sound with the ear
Learn information, be informed
Listen attentively, lend an ear
Obey, submit to
Make a sound, produce a voice
Announce, proclaim, publish
H8085I.detail:
1. Physically perceiving sounds with the ear: this is the simple act of listening to what comes to our ears. In Judges 13:23, Manoah's wife says: "He would not have now made us hear such things," meaning conveyed these audible words.

2. Learning information, being informed, or receiving news: the meaning extends from the physical act of hearing to understanding the message. One "hears about" something that one learns from a distance.

3. Listening attentively, voluntarily lending an ear, showing interest: this means hearing in the sense of wanting to listen, being open to a word.

4. Obeying, submitting to an authority or request: "to hear" in the biblical sense includes the idea of being persuaded and acting accordingly. It is the obedience of the heart that follows the listening of the ear.

5. Making a sound, producing a loud voice: in an active sense, it is causing the sound to be heard by others. In 1 Chronicles 15:28, Israel makes "the lutes and harps sound."

6. Announcing publicly, proclaiming, making known: the verb expresses the action of one who raises their voice so that all may hear and know. In Isaiah 52:7, one "publishes" peace and salvation.
H8085I.origine: This verb comes from a common Hebrew root that first evokes the physical action of listening, then expands to the idea of obeying and understanding. The word carries the conviction that true listening leads to obedience. Several biblical passages play on this double meaning: hearing the message of the Lord and submitting to it go together. The family of the word includes terms related to voice, sound, and the action of making known.
H8085I.emploi: This verb is one of the most common in the Old Testament (46 occurrences in the provided list). It appears strongly among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos) where it means to announce, proclaim, or publish aloud. In historical narratives (Judges, Samuel, Chronicles), it primarily expresses the act of listening and obeying. The Psalms use it to recount the works of God or to burst forth in praise. The meaning gradually shifts: it can denote first the simple auditory perception, then attention, then obedience, and finally public announcement. Isaiah uses the verb to say that the prophets "foretell" or "proclaim," meaning they make the divine word resound.
H8085I.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that true listening to God involves obedience, not passive hearing. When one "hears" the divine word in the Bible, one is called to respond with life. It is also a word of hope: God hears the cries and prayers of His people (Psalms 76:9), which means He is aware of them and responds.

sens: Perceive a sound or word by the ear
Understand the meaning of a language or speech
Listen attentively, pay attention to
Obey, consent to what is said
Be heard, have a voice that resonates
H8085J.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: to perceive a voice or noise by the ear. When Moses says that one will not 'hear' the language of a distant nation (Deuteronomy 28:49), he means that one will not perceive the distinct sounds of that foreign language.

2. But 'hear' goes further: it means to grasp the meaning, to truly understand. Joseph 'understood' the language of his brothers, as the text states in Genesis 42:23 — not only did he hear the sounds, but he grasped their meaning. Similarly, an 'understanding' heart (1 Kings 3:9) is a heart that truly hears, discerns, and understands.

3. The verb also means 'to listen with interest,' to give attention. It is to listen for real, not just to let a noise pass by.

4. Ultimately, hearing leads to obedience: when one truly hears the voice of God, one can only consent to it and submit to it.

5. The word can also refer to the action of being heard: a voice that resonates, that reaches the ear of another.
H8085J.origine: The root is very ancient in Hebrew. It primarily evokes the physical act of perceiving a sound by the ear. But very quickly, in biblical usage, it enriches: to hear is to understand, then to obey. This progression of meaning — from the physical to the moral — is typical of Hebrew thought, which does not separate action from intention. In biblical Hebrew, one 'hears' to understand and to act, never passively.
H8085J.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the provided usages, often to emphasize the understanding of a foreign language. In Genesis 11:7, during the Tower of Babel, God confuses the languages 'so that they will not hear' — meaning they will not understand. In Genesis 42:23, Joseph 'understood' Hebrew while speaking through an interpreter. In 1 Kings 3:9, Solomon asks for an 'understanding' heart to judge — here the word takes on a moral nuance: it is the ability to discern good from evil, to truly understand. The context shows that 'to hear' can mean 'to be attentive to,' 'to lend an ear to,' or even 'to obey.' Other passages (Jeremiah 5:15, Ezekiel 3:6) confirm that the word applies to the challenge of understanding a strange language or message.
H8085J.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that faith is never purely auditory or intellectual: 'to hear' the Word of God is to truly understand it, to grasp it in the heart, and ultimately to obey it.
