The New Testament will take up this idea ('he who has ears to hear, let him hear'). This verb invites a lively, attentive listening that engages the whole person.

sens: Perceive by hearing a sound, a voice, or a word
Listen attentively, pay attention to someone
Understand the meaning of a word or language
Accept, consent to what is requested
Judge, resolve a dispute by listening to the parties
Obey, submit to an instruction or order
H8085K.detail:
1. Perceive by hearing a sound, a voice, or a word: this is the simplest and most common physical meaning of the word. The ear receives a sound vibration and the brain recognizes it.

2. Listen attentively, pay attention to someone: go beyond simple perception to add the intention of receiving what is said. In Judges 11:10, the elders ask the Lord to 'hear' them, meaning to truly listen, to pay attention to their words.

3. Understand the meaning of a word or language: to hear does not stop at sounds, but touches the intelligence of what is communicated. To grasp the message behind the words.

4. Accept, consent to what is requested: when one truly listens to someone, one can accept their words. It is the heart that receives and adheres.

5. Judge, resolve a dispute by listening to the parties: in 1 Kings 3:11, Solomon asks for discernment to 'exercise' justice, meaning to listen to the complaints and render a just judgment. The judge must first hear before deciding.

6. Obey, submit to an instruction or order: when one truly hears the word of God or an authority, the next step is to obey it and put it into practice. To hear becomes synonymous with obedience.
H8085K.origine: The Hebrew word šāmaʿ likely comes from an onomatopoeic root, imitating the sound of the ear straining to hear. The family of this word includes several forms: the Qal (simple form) for the basic action of hearing or listening, the Niphal for the act of being heard, the Piel for 'making heard' or 'calling to hear,' and the Hiphil for 'proclaiming' or 'announcing.' This diversity of forms shows how the concept of listening unfolds in everyday life: one hears, is heard, calls someone to listen, proclaims a message. It is one of the most common verbs in the Hebrew Bible, at the heart of the relationship between God and His people.
H8085K.emploi: The verb šāmaʿ appears several hundred times in the Old Testament. It primarily denotes the physical act of hearing a sound or voice, but very quickly it transcends this framework to express a whole range of nuances: listening attentively, consenting, accepting, obeying. In the Bible, to hear is never passive; it always involves responsibility. In Judges 11:10, the elders ask the Lord to 'hear' them, which means both to listen and to take their words into account, thus helping them. In 1 Kings 3:11, the verb takes on the shade of 'discerning' or 'exercising just judgment': Solomon wants to 'hear' the cases to judge wisely. Both usages show how the word climbs a scale from the concrete (perceiving a noise) to the abstract (rendering justice) through attentive listening and consent.
H8085K.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the relationship with God is never closed or solitary: God listens to the prayers of His people. But it also emphasizes that 'to hear' implies responsibility: one who hears the word of God cannot remain neutral. To hear is also to obey. The biblical text invites everyone to cultivate an attentive ear to the voice of God, beyond the superficial sounds of the world.

sens: Perceive a sound by the ear
Listen attentively, pay attention
Understand the meaning of what is said
Receive favorably, consent to a request
Obey, be attentive to an instruction
H8085L.detail:
1. Perceive a sound by the ear: this is the simplest and most direct meaning of the verb. It refers to the physical ability to capture noises, voices, or words through hearing.
2. Listen attentively, pay attention: to hear does not only mean to passively capture sounds, but also to welcome them with interest. It is to truly listen to someone, to give them your attention. Hezekiah "listened to" the envoys from Babylon (2 Kings 20:13), meaning he listened to and received them.
3. Understand the meaning of what is said: to hear also means to grasp and understand language, not just raw sounds.
4. Receive favorably, consent to a request: when one hears someone in this sense, one approves their words and accepts what they ask for. It is to give one's agreement.
5. Obey, be attentive to an instruction: to hear a word can mean to put it into practice, to conform one's life to it. This is the deepest form of listening in the Bible.
H8085L.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁמַע (shamaʿ) is one of the most fundamental in the Hebrew Bible. It comes from a root that evokes the physical act of listening. In biblical Hebrew, hearing is often linked not only to audition but to a reaction: one does not listen passively, one responds. The word is very frequent in all the books of the Old Testament, particularly in contexts of obedience to God, communication between people, or proclamation.
H8085L.emploi: This verb is extremely common in the Hebrew Bible, where it appears several hundred times. It is used to describe: the act of listening to a voice or a noise; the listening of a person who reports news ("hear say"); the consent to a prayer or a request; obedience to God or to an authority. In 2 Kings 20:13, Hezekiah "listened to" the envoys of the king of Babylon means that he listened to them attentively and received them in an official audience. The word can also refer to the noise or sound itself (nominal sense).
H8085L.portee: In biblical Hebrew, "hearing" is never a passive or neutral act: it is always engaged listening, which calls for a response. For the believer, this word reminds us that faith begins with listening — listening to the Word of God. To hear God is not only to receive His message but also to consent to it and obey it. It is a call to the responsibility of the one who listens.

sens: Perceive a sound by the ear
Learn news, be informed
Obey, show attentiveness to a word
H8086.detail:
1. Perceive a sound by the ear: this is the simplest meaning of the word. When King Nebuchadnezzar gives the order, people must bow "when you hear the sound of the trumpet, the flute, the harp" (Daniel 3:5). The verb describes the physical act of listening and receiving a noise or a voice.

2. Learn news, be informed: the word extends to the sense of receiving information, becoming aware of something through hearsay. When Darius says to Daniel, "I have learned that you have the spirit of the gods in you" (Daniel 5:14), the verb "hear" refers to having known, having received this information through communication.

3. Obey, show attentiveness to a word: beyond simple hearing, "to hear" can mean to accept a word, to respond to it, to submit to it. It is less about passive listening than about active receptivity to an order or message.
H8086.origine: The word שְׁמַע (shema) comes from a very ancient root in Semitic, common to Hebrew and Aramaic, which expresses the idea of receiving through the ear. The same root is found in the Shema Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4 in Hebrew), the fundamental prayer of Judaism: "Hear, O Israel". The word always invites a conscious reception, never purely passive: to hear is to welcome and respond.
H8086.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 9 times in the book of Daniel, mainly in chapter 3 (5 occurrences) where the king orders the worship of the golden statue "when you hear the sound of the instruments". The first three uses (Daniel 3:5, 3:7, 3:10) show people who truly listen to this order and bow down. Daniel 3:15 repeats the order with a threat. In chapter 5, the word shifts towards the meaning of "learn" when Darius reports what he has heard about Daniel's powers. Each time, "to hear" engages the listener: it is never neutral, it always leads to an action or a decision.
H8086.portee: For the believer, this word invites reflection on the quality of our listening. To hear is not just a passive act of the ear; it is to welcome a word with our whole being. The context of Daniel also reminds us that our obedience to the word of God must take precedence over the orders of the powerful: the three Hebrews "heard" the king's order, but they did not obey, for their true obedience was to God alone.

sens: Son of Hebron, of the tribe of Judah, during the divided monarchy
H8087G.detail: Shema is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb. He is the son of Hebron and the father of Racham. He is found in the list of Hebron's children, alongside his brothers Korah, Tappuah, and Rekem (1 Chronicles 2:43). His son Racham is himself the father of Jorkeam (1 Chronicles 2:44).
H8087G.origine: The name Shema means "hear" or "he has heard" in Hebrew, derived from the root שמע which evokes the act of hearing and obeying. This same root is found in the phrase "Shema Israel", the call to listen that is at the heart of Jewish prayer.
H8087G.emploi: Shema appears twice in Chronicles, only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2, where the descendants of Judah through the line of Caleb are enumerated. These verses aim to establish the precise lineage between families and generations during the period of the divided monarchy. He is a minor genealogical figure, mentioned only for his place in this chain of ancestors.

sens: A man of the tribe of Reuben during the divided monarchy
H8087H.detail: 1. Shema is a Reubenite mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:8. He is the son of Joel and the father of Azaz, which also makes him the grandfather of Bela. His name means "hear" in Hebrew, but he is mentioned here only to establish the genealogy of the Reubenites, with no events from his life reported.
H8087H.origine: The name Shema comes from the Hebrew שׁמע (shama), which literally means "hear" or "listen". It is a common verb in the Bible to denote the act of listening, particularly in the expression of the Shema Yisrael ("Hear, O Israel"), which is the great monotheistic profession of faith of Israel in Deuteronomy 6:4. The name thus evokes the idea of a person who listens or hears, which was an important quality in Israelite culture.
H8087H.emploi: Shema appears only once in the canonical Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:8. There he is presented in a genealogical list of the descendants of Reuben, son of Jacob. These genealogical lists in the book of Chronicles aim to preserve the memory of the structure of the Israelite tribes at different periods. Shema represents here a link in a genealogical chain that shows how the tribe of Reuben developed over generations. His only role in the biblical text is to connect his father Joel to his son Azaz and his grandson Bela.

sens: Benjamite, son of Elpahal, family leader in Ajalon
H8087I.detail: 1. Schema is a man from the tribe of Benjamin living during the time of the divided monarchy. He was the son of Elpahal and, along with his brother Beria, was a family leader among the inhabitants of Ajalon. These two brothers together drove out the inhabitants of Gath from their region (1 Chronicles 8:13).
H8087I.origine: The name Schema means "Hear" or "Listen" in Hebrew, derived from the root שׁמע (to hear, to listen). It was a common name among the Israelites, and several men in the Old Testament bore it, including a Reubenite and a Judean according to genealogies.
H8087I.emploi: Schema appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:13, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented as one of the family leaders who played an active role in defending their territory by expelling the inhabitants of Gath. This is the only context in which this man is mentioned in Scripture.

sens: A figure who assisted Ezra during the reading of the Law to the people of Israel after the Exile
H8087J.detail: 1. Schema is an Israelite mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. He stood to the right of Ezra the scribe when he read the Law before the assembled people in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. His presence among Ezra's assistants suggests that he held a position of authority or responsibility in the community's reconstruction.
H8087J.origine: The name Schema means "Listen" or "He has heard" in Hebrew, derived from the root that expresses the idea of hearing and listening. This same verb is famous in the Shema Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4), the central prayer of Judaism. The name reflects the importance of listening and obedience to God's word, fundamental values of biblical faith.
H8087J.emploi: Schema appears only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. He is among the Levites or leaders of the people who assisted Ezra during the solemn ceremony where the Law was read to the crowd of Israelites returned from captivity. This unique mention places him at a key moment in Israel's history: the religious and national restoration after the Babylonian exile, around the 5th century BCE.

sens: That produces a loud and clear sound
That resonates, that echoes
That strikes the ear with its power
H8088A.detail:
1. This word describes something that produces a perceptible, loud, and well-articulated sound. The "sounding" cymbals of Psalms 150:5 are those that create a loud and distinct noise, capable of filling a place and being heard by all.
2. The image is one of something that resonates, that spreads — the sound does not remain muffled but bursts forth with energy. It is the opposite of a dull or muffled noise.
3. The word emphasizes intensity and clarity: what is sound is meant to be heard, to strike the ear with impact. In the context of the psalm, praising God "with sounding cymbals" means expressing praise with all the power and liveliness one possesses.
H8088A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root (שׁמע) that fundamentally means "to hear" or "to listen." But here, it designates what produces a sound to be heard: it is the transition from the verb (to hear) to the noun (that which is heard). The word belongs to the vocabulary of auditory perception and noisy manifestation.
H8088A.emploi: This word appears once in the Bible, in Psalms 150:5, in the context of praise in the sanctuary. The psalm lists all the instruments that should praise God, and it specifically characterizes the cymbals by this sound quality — they should not be mute or silent, but produce a resounding sound. It is a call to total praise, where even the instruments loudly express the glory of God.
H8088A.portee: This word reminds us that praising God is not a discreet or shameful matter: it must resound, be heard, and manifest with strength the joy and gratitude of the heart. For the Christian, it is an invitation to express faith without timidity, with all the liveliness and energy one possesses, without fear of disturbing.

sens: What is said, what is reported about someone or something
The information, the news that spreads
The reputation, the glory known from afar
The echo, the impact produced by someone's renown
H8088B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is said, the noise made about it: when Laban learns the news concerning Jacob, he is so moved that he runs to meet him (Genesis 29:13). It is the information that circulates, what is reported.
2. By extension, it is the news itself, the announcement of an event that spreads: in Isaiah 23:5, the Egyptians tremble when they learn of the fall of Tyre — it is the concrete news that reaches them.
3. When this noise speaks of someone great, it becomes fame, reputation, glory: the queen of Sheba heard about Solomon's fame, so great that she wants to meet him (1 Kings 10:1). The word then evokes what is known about a person, the consideration they enjoy.
4. In some cases, it designates the impact, the effect produced by someone: the peoples tremble upon hearing of God's deeds, so impressive is His renown (Numbers 14:15).
H8088B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to hear, to listen." Shemuah literally means "that which is heard" — the noise that is heard circulating. This name is related to the verb "to listen": one speaks of someone, one hears it said, and from there fame is born. It is what enters through the ear and spreads from mouth to mouth.
H8088B.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Bible, mainly to designate what is said or known about a famous person. Laban learns the news of Jacob (Genesis 29:13), the queen of Sheba comes because of Solomon's fame (1 Kings 10:1). The word can also name event-related news: that of the fall of Tyre alarms Egypt (Isaiah 23:5), that of Pharaoh's march stops the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 37:5). Sometimes it describes the impact or fear that someone inspires: the peoples who have heard of God are seized with fear. It is always information that travels, that has weight.
H8088B.portee: This word reminds us that fame and reputation rest on what is said about them — they live by the word that spreads. For the believer, this sheds light on how God's glory is known: not through a direct and universal experience, but through the testimony that travels from mouth to mouth. It is a call to be mindful of what is said about a person, a work, or God Himself.

sens: What is said, what is told about someone or something
The reputation, the buzz that someone or something creates in the land
The fame, the celebrity that grows and spreads
The news, the information that comes from afar
The buzz of news, the echoes that spread
H8089.detail: 1. What is said, what is told about someone: it is the information, the story that circulates. When the Gibeonite servants say to Joshua, "we have heard about him, about all that he did in Egypt" (Joshua 9:9), they refer to the stories, the news that are transmitted from one place to another. 2. Reputation, prestige: it is the way one is known, spoken of in a country. The fame of Joshua "spread throughout the land" (Joshua 6:27), just as that of Mordecai "spread in all the provinces" (Esther 9:4), showing that their name grows and that everyone talks about them. 3. The news that arrives: in Jeremiah 6:24, "at the sound of their approach," this word refers to the echo, the news of the enemy's arrival that reaches the ears and sows anxiety. It is the information heard from afar that provokes an immediate reaction.
H8089.origine: This word comes from a root that means to listen, to hear (שׁמע, shama), and it retains the image: what is heard, what reaches the ears. It is a variant of a very similar word. Its core is the idea of transmission by word and hearing: one reports what one has heard, one circulates the news.
H8089.emploi: This word appears four times in the Old Testament, always to evoke a reputation, a buzz, a news that spreads. It especially characterizes the growing celebrity of a powerful or victorious figure: Joshua whose fame grows after the capture of Jericho, Mordecai whose power and reputation increase at the king's palace. It can also simply designate the news, the information heard, like the echo of the enemy's approach that sows terror. The word always suggests a dynamic phenomenon: something that spreads, that grows, that acts on those who hear it.
H8089.portee: This word reminds us that reputation and fame spread by word of mouth. It is an invitation to understand that our actions and our faithfulness become known, that God Himself makes Himself known through His works and the story that is told about them. For the believer, it raises the question: what reputation do my life and actions build around me?

sens: City of Judah located at the southern border of the territory towards Edom
H8090.detail: Schema is a small fortified city in the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah during the land distribution after the conquest of Canaan. It appears in the list of cities in the Negev, the desert region of southern Judah, established in Joshua 15:26, where it is mentioned between Amam and Moladah.
H8090.origine: The name literally means "listen" or "hearing" (root שׁמע, "to hear"), sharing its root with biblical words expressing the action of listening or sound. This place name, like many in Canaan, likely evokes a remarkable event or a characteristic of the site known to the ancient inhabitants.
H8090.emploi: Schema appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:26, in the enumeration of the cities of the Negev assigned to Judah. It plays no narrative role in the biblical account and is mentioned only as a geographical landmark in the cadastration of the tribal territory.

sens: Elite warrior in the service of King David
H8091.detail: Schama is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the most powerful warriors of King David are listed. He was the son of Hotham and brother of Jehiel, both from Aroer. These three men — Uzziah, Schama, and Jehiel — form a group of elite warriors integrated into David's army, proof of the fame and prestige enjoyed by certain warrior families in the kingdom of Israel at that time.
H8091.origine: The name Schama means "obedient" in Hebrew, derived from the root that expresses listening and obedience. This name reflects the values of the loyal warrior who listens and obeys the orders of his king.
H8091.emploi: Schama appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:44, in the midst of a long list of David's most valiant warriors. This list, known as "the Thirty" or "the Mighty Men of David," enumerates the military leaders who contributed to the greatness of David's reign and the stability of his kingdom.

sens: Levite of the lineage of Gershon, father of Berachiah
H8092G.detail: Schimea is a man of the tribe of Levi mentioned only once in the Bible. He belongs to the descendants of Gershon, one of the three sons of Levi. He is the father of Berachiah and the grandfather of Asaph, who became a famous musician of the temple (1 Chronicles 6:30).
H8092G.origine: The Hebrew name שִׁמְעָא (Schimea) means "fame" or "what is heard." It derives from the root שׁמע (chama), which means "to hear" or "to listen." This name evokes the idea of an established reputation or a name that spreads. Several biblical characters bear this name or similar variants (Schimma, Schimea).
H8092G.emploi: Schimea appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 6:30, where he is listed in the genealogy of the Levites responsible for the temple service. He is part of the genealogical line that leads to Asaph, one of the three chief musicians of worship under King David. This presence in the genealogical records of the Levites underscores his role in the continuity of divine service, even though no specific details about his life are provided.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, father of Berechiah and grandfather of Asaph
H8092H.detail: Schimea is a Levite from the family of the Gershonites mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:39. He is presented as the father of Berechiah and the grandfather of the famous temple musician Asaph, who "stood at the right" of the choir during worship. His name means "fame" in Hebrew, but it is primarily his role in the priestly and musical genealogy of Israel that defines him: he belongs to this Levitical line responsible for the songs of the temple.
H8092H.origine: The name Schimea comes from the Hebrew שִׁמְעָא (shim'ah), built on the root שׁמע (shema, "to hear") or שׁם (shem, "name, fame"). The primary meaning is "fame" or "one who is spoken of." Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, including a son of David, but this one in the Levitical genealogy is distinct. The family of the Gershonites to which he belongs is an important branch of the Levites responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple.
H8092H.emploi: Schimea appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:39, in the context of the genealogy of the temple musicians. He is mentioned as the father of Berechiah and grandfather of Asaph, one of the three great musicians of Israel under King David. This passage enumerates the genealogies of the Levites responsible for singing in the temple, showing how Asaph, responsible for sacred music, came from a respectable line of Gershonite Levites. This single mention is enough to place him in the religious history of Israel.

sens: Son of Jesse, third son and brother of David
Father of Jonadab
H8092I.detail:
1. Schimea is the third son of Jesse, the father of David. He appears in the genealogy of David's family in 1 Chronicles 2:13, where he is listed among Jesse's sons along with his brothers Eliab and Abinadab. The same man is mentioned under different names in other passages: Shammah in 1 Samuel 16:9 and Shimeah in 1 Chronicles 20:7.
2. Schimea is the father of Jonadab. He is seen in 1 Chronicles 20:7, where his son Jonathan (another form of the name Jonadab) confronts and kills a giant, thus performing an act of bravery for Israel.
H8092I.origine: The name Schimea comes from Hebrew and means "fame" or "celebrity." It is a family name that marks the importance of Jesse's lineage, from which King David descends. The same man bears several names in the biblical texts (Shammah, Shimea, Shimeah), which is common in ancient Hebrew narratives.
H8092I.emploi: Schimea appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a member of David's royal family. Although few details are given about his personal life, his mention in these genealogical passages shows that he held an important place in the Davidic genealogy. His son Jonathan is famous for killing a giant warrior, which speaks volumes about the valor of his descendants. Schimea is thus primarily known as David's brother and the father of a valiant warrior.
H8092I.portee: Schimea reminds us that David's genealogy is not only that of a great king but of an entire family where courage and virtue are passed down from generation to generation. His son Jonathan perpetuates his father's honor by performing acts of bravery, showing how faith and strength of character are reflected in the descendants.

sens: son of David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem
H8092J.detail: Schimea is one of the sons that David had with Bathsheba in Jerusalem, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:5 among the four children born from this union (the other three being Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon). He is also cited in 2 Samuel 5:14 under the same name. Although little information is given about his personal life, he represents the royal lineage of David and fits into the genealogy of the king.
H8092J.origine: The name Schimea means "fame" or "celebrity." It comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the notion of "name" or "reputation" — an appropriate image for a son of King David, whose family was known throughout Israel. The same man is referred to as Schammua in 1 Chronicles 3:5: these two names refer to the same person.
H8092J.emploi: Schimea appears only once in the Segond (1 Chronicles 3:5) within the genealogical list of David's sons born in Jerusalem. He is presented as one of the four children of David and Bathsheba, alongside Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. This unique biblical mention places him in the context of royal succession, without additional details about his role or life. He should not be confused with the other Schimea mentioned elsewhere in the Bible: a brother of David, son of Jesse, and a Gershonite Levite.

sens: Brother of David, son of Jesse
Father of Jonadab and Jonathan
H8093.detail:
1. Schimea is a son of Jesse and the brother of David, living during the time of the united monarchy of Israel. He is first mentioned in the accounts surrounding King David, particularly for his remarkable descendants.
2. Schimea is the father of Jonadab, a very skilled man and advisor to King Amnon (2 Samuel 13:3), and of Jonathan, who killed a giant that challenged Israel (2 Samuel 21:21). His descendants play important roles in royal history.
H8093.origine: The name Schimea means "celebrity" or "fame" in Hebrew. It comes from the root that evokes what is heard or known, suggesting someone whose renown extends. This character is also called Schammah or Schimma in other passages (1 Samuel 16:9; 1 Chronicles 2:13), variations of the same name reflecting different ways of transcribing it.
H8093.emploi: Schimea appears three times in the accounts of the Hebrew Bible (2 Samuel 13:3, 13:32, 21:21), always designated as "brother of David." He is best known as the father of important figures: Jonadab, who plays a role with King Amnon and demonstrates sagacity in deducing what really happened after Amnon's death, and Jonathan, whose name evokes a valiant warrior killing a giant. These mentions place him in the royal sphere and show his role as the patriarch of an influential lineage.

sens: Father of two warriors who joined David at Ziklag
H8094.detail: Schemaa is a man from Gibeah, in Benjamin, whose two sons, Ahi-ezer and Joash, were powerful warriors. These two men are among those who rallied to David at Ziklag, according to 1 Chronicles 12:3.
H8094.origine: The name Schemaa means "the rumor" or "what is heard" in Hebrew, formed from the root that expresses the idea of listening or news that spreads.
H8094.emploi: Schemaa appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:3, where he is identified as the father of Ahi-ezer and Joash. These two sons are presented as valiant warriors who joined David during his stay at Ziklag, before he became king. This passage places Schemaa among the Benjaminite families that supported David.

sens: Second son of Jacob and Leah
Tribe of Israel descended from Simeon
Territory allocated to the tribe of Simeon
H8095G.detail:
1. Simeon is the second son born to Jacob by his wife Leah. His name means "God has heard," as Leah named him saying: "The Lord has heard that I am unloved" (Genesis 29:33). Along with his brothers, he will participate in the patriarch's life, notably in the incident against Shechem (Genesis 34:25) and will be recognized among the twelve sons of Israel during the departure to Egypt (Exodus 1:2).
2. The tribe of Simeon is formed by the descendants of Simeon and includes his six sons: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zerah, and Shaul (Genesis 46:10). In the wilderness, it is organized into clans and receives leaders and military personnel (Numbers 1:22-23, Numbers 26:12).
3. The territory of Simeon, allocated during the conquest of Canaan, is located in the south and entirely within the lands of Judah, as Judah's share was too large (Joshua 19:1-9). The tribe of Simeon thus does not possess an autonomous territory but lives enclosed within that of Judah.
H8095G.origine: The Hebrew name Shim'on comes from the root that means "to listen" or "to hear." Leah chose this name to commemorate the fact that God had listened to her prayer and her distress as a less-loved woman. This name thus expresses gratitude to the Lord who hears the cries of those who suffer.
H8095G.emploi: Simeon appears 38 times in the provided biblical usages, from the Pentateuch to the historical and prophetic books. He is first mentioned at his birth (Genesis 29:33), then in the genealogies of Jacob's twelve sons (Exodus 1:2, 1 Chronicles 2:1). The tribe bears his name throughout the Old Testament: it receives its organization during the census in the wilderness (Numbers 1:6, Numbers 1:22-23), its territorial inheritance during the conquest (Joshua 19:1-9), and its warriors are counted in military accounts (Judges 1:3, 1 Chronicles 4:42). It also figures in the prophetic promises of Israel's borders (Ezekiel 48:24-25).
H8095G.portee: Simeon reminds us that God hears the cries of those who suffer and seek help. His story within the people of Israel illustrates how a tribe receives its inheritance and place within God's people, even if it is not the largest (Joshua 19:9). For the Christian reader, this name invites trust in a God attentive to the prayers of His children.

sens: Israelite during the time of Ezra who married a foreign woman
H8095H.detail: 1. He is an Israelite who lived during the time of the return from exile, after the Babylonian captivity. He belonged to the family of the sons of Bani and was among those who had taken a foreign wife — which was considered contrary to the law of Moses. Ezra 10:31 mentions him in the list of those who agreed to send away their foreign wives to conform to God's will.
H8095H.origine: The name Simeon comes from Hebrew and means "one who has heard" or "heard by God." It is formed from the root "to listen," evoking the idea that God has listened, or that the child was given in response to a heard prayer. This name was borne in antiquity by several important figures in Israel, notably the second son of Jacob.
H8095H.emploi: Simeon is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:31. He appears in the list of Israelite men who, upon returning from exile in Babylon, had married women from foreign peoples. Under Ezra's leadership, these men agreed to separate from their wives to restore the purity of God's people according to the Mosaic Law. His case illustrates the moral and religious challenges that the returning community had to face.
H8095H.portee: The story of Simeon and his companions shows how God calls His people to repent and separate from what contravenes His will, even at the cost of difficult personal sacrifices. It is a concrete illustration of spiritual restoration and the obedience that follows the judgment of exile.

sens: son of Gershon and grandson of Levi
ancestor of the Shimeites family, a branch of the Levites
H8096G.detail: Shimei is a man of the tribe of Levi, son of Gershon and grandson of Levi, living during the time of Egypt and the wilderness. He first appears in Exodus 6:17 as one of the two sons of Gershon (along with Libni). His own sons — Jachath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah — in turn found an important Levitical lineage (1 Chronicles 23:10). His descendants become a recognized branch of the Levites, the Shimeites, who play a role in the service of the tabernacle and the temple.
H8096G.origine: The name Shimei means "renowned" or "one who hears." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing fame or renown. In the genealogy of the people of Israel, this name becomes the name of an entire Levitical house, recalling the importance of this ancestor in the organization of Israelite worship.
H8096G.emploi: Shimei is mentioned only in the genealogical passages of Exodus and First Chronicles. In Exodus 6:17 and Numbers 3:18, he is presented as the second son of Gershon. In 1 Chronicles 6:17 and 23:7, these genealogical lists are repeated to recall the Levitical descent. In 1 Chronicles 23:10, his four sons are listed, thus establishing the subdivisions of this Levitical branch. These passages show that Shimei is known primarily through his posterity and his role as a founding ancestor of a lineage of worship servants.

sens: Benjamite of the house of Saul who cursed David during his flight
Man who asked forgiveness from David and received grace from him
Servant of King Solomon subject to a condition and who violated it
H8096H.detail:
1. Shimei is first known as a member of the royal family of Saul. When David flees from Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion, Shimei pursues him, cursing, throwing stones and dust at him (2 Samuel 16:5, 16:13). This is an act of vengeance: the house of Saul sees David as the usurper of the throne they have lost.
2. After David's victory, Shimei completely changes his attitude. He prostrates himself before the king and asks for forgiveness (2 Samuel 19:18). David, magnanimous, swears to him that he will not die (2 Samuel 19:23), granting grace to this former enemy who acknowledges his wrongdoing.
3. Under Solomon's reign, the king imposes a condition on Shimei: to remain in Jerusalem without leaving the city (1 Kings 2:36). Three years later, Shimei violates this order by pursuing two escaped servants, which leads to his death sentence (1 Kings 2:39-44). His story shows that granted grace requires faithfulness.
H8096H.origine: The name Shimei means "renowned" or "illustrious" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes fame and honor. It is a name borne by several men in the Bible, notably Levites, but the most famous Shimei is this Benjamite of the house of Saul.
H8096H.emploi: Shimei appears mainly in the story of David and Solomon (2 Samuel 16—19 and 1 Kings 2). At first (2 Samuel 16), he is a fierce enemy who curses the king in exile. The episode at the Jordan (2 Samuel 19) shows his dramatic repentance: he acknowledges David as legitimate. Solomon places him under a sort of house arrest, allowing him to live but depriving him of freedom. When Shimei breaks this condition in 1 Kings 2:39-44, he seals his fate. His story illustrates how David and Solomon treat their enemies: first with clemency and grace, then, in the face of recidivism, with justice.
H8096H.portee: The account of Shimei teaches that divine (and human) grace is never a permission to continue in wrongdoing. David forgives and spares Shimei, but this forgiveness comes with a condition that tests his true conversion. Shimei's final transgression shows that rejecting granted grace leads to just consequences. For the believer, it is a call to gratitude for the mercy received and to the faithfulness it demands.

sens: Benjamite, son of Ela, officer in Solomon's administration
Benjamite, son of Gera, of the house of Saul, during David's time
H8096I.detail:
1. Shimei first refers to a Benjamite officer in the service of King Solomon, son of Ela (1 Kings 4:18). He was responsible for the royal palace's provisions in his region.
2. The name also refers to a Benjamite of the house of Saul, son of Gera, who remained loyal to David during the revolt of Adonijah (1 Kings 1:8): he was among the important figures of the united kingdom who supported Solomon rather than the pretender to the throne.
H8096I.origine: The name Shimei comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be famous" or "to have renown." It appears several times in the Old Testament to designate different people: a Levite son of Gershon, a chief of singers, and other servants of worship or the crown. The persistence of the name in the narrative of the united monarchy shows its importance in the influential families of Israel.
H8096I.emploi: The word Shimei designates at least two distinct characters in the uses of the Segond. The first is mentioned in 1 Kings 4:18 as the son of Ela and a commissariat officer in Benjamin, responsible for the provisions of Solomon's palace. The second appears in 1 Kings 1:8 as a Benjamite of the house of Saul, son of Gera, who supported Solomon and did not join Adonijah's rebellion. These two figures illustrate how the name was borne by influential men at the heart of royal power in Israel.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H8096J.detail: 1. Shimei is a man of the tribe of Judah who lived at the time when the kingdom of Israel had divided into two kingdoms (the Northern and Southern kingdoms). He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:19, where he is designated as one of the sons of Pedahiah.
H8096J.origine: The name Shimei means "renowned" or "one who hears." It is a fairly common Hebrew name in the Old Testament, borne by many people — notably a cousin of King David, a Levitical musician, and an officer under King Solomon. Each of these Shimeis is a different person. This one, son of Pedahiah, is the latest chronologically.
H8096J.emploi: Shimei, son of Pedahiah, appears only once in Scripture: in 1 Chronicles 3:19. He is mentioned as one of the sons of Pedahiah and brother of Zerubbabel, the man who led the return of the Jews from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem. His existence is known to us only through this royal genealogy recorded in the chronicles of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H8096K.detail: 1. Schimeï is a man of the tribe of Simeon, son of Zaccur, mentioned for the first time in 1 Chronicles 4:26. He belongs to a genealogy of the tribe of Simeon and is part of the history of Israel during the period of the divided monarchy, after the schism between the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom. According to 1 Chronicles 4:27, Schimeï had sixteen sons and six daughters, which attests to his numerous descendants and his importance in his tribe.
H8096K.origine: The name Schimeï means "illustrious" or "renowned" in Hebrew. It comes from a root expressing fame or glory. This name was borne by several men in the history of Israel, including Levites and other members of different tribes, all significant in the religious and political structure of the people.
H8096K.emploi: Schimeï appears twice in the Segond 1910: in 1 Chronicles 4:26 and 4:27. He is presented as the son of Zaccur, son of Mischma, in the genealogy of Simeon. The text emphasizes that unlike his brothers whose families did not multiply much, Schimeï had a numerous posterity with sixteen sons and six daughters, which distinguishes him in the tribal lineage and shows the divine blessing on his descendants.

sens: Man of the tribe of Reuben during the time of the divided monarchy
H8096L.detail: Schimeï is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, but this one specifically refers to a Reubenite, son of Gog and father of Michah, mentioned only once in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben (1 Chronicles 5:4).
H8096L.origine: The name Schimeï means "renowned" or "he who has heard." It is borne by about sixteen different characters in the Old Testament, which shows its common usage among the Israelites. The name Shimei or its variants (Shimhi, Shimi) notably appear among the Levites — several temple servants and musicians bear this name — and among the Benjamites, particularly in the house of Saul.
H8096L.emploi: Schimeï is the name of a Reubenite who is part of the genealogical lineage of his tribe: he is the son of Gog and the father of Michah. This genealogy is documented in 1 Chronicles 5:4 during the enumeration of the descendants of Reuben. Although not well known, this Schimeï is part of the recognized ancestors of Israel and helps to reconstruct the history of the tribes after the division of the kingdom.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Libni, living during the time of the divided monarchy
H8096M.detail: Schimeï is a Levite, a member of the priestly family of Israel. He is the son of Libni and the father of Uzzah, according to the genealogy of the descendants of Merari reported in 1 Chronicles 6:29. He lived during the period of the divided monarchy, a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between two rival kingdoms. His name means "renowned" or "illustrious" in Hebrew.
H8096M.origine: The name Schimeï (שִׁמְעִי) comes from the Hebrew root that evokes notoriety or fame. Several men bore this name in ancient Israel, all from important genealogies: Levites, Benjamites, Simeonites, and others. The name reflects the importance of genealogical lineages among the people of God, where each name was linked to an identity and a function.
H8096M.emploi: This particular Schimeï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:29, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Merari (one of the three sons of Levi). This genealogy precisely situates his place in the priestly system of Israel. Unlike other Schimeï mentioned in Scripture (notably the Benjamite who cursed David), this one is known only by his place in this genealogical succession. The name Schimeï appears about 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, designating various people of different conditions and times.

sens: Benjamite father of several sons
Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H8096N.detail: 1. Schimeï is a Benjamite, that is, a man from the tribe of Benjamin in Israel. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:21 as the father of Adajah, Beriah, and Shimrath, making him an ancestor in the genealogy of the Benjamites.
H8096N.origine: The name Schimeï means "renowned" or "he who hears." It is a common Hebrew name during the monarchical period, borne by several figures in the history of Israel. The text of 1 Chronicles places him in the genealogical lineage of the descendants of Benjamin.
H8096N.emploi: Schimeï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:21, in a genealogical list of the Benjamites. He is identified as the father of three sons: Adajah, Beriah, and Shimrath. This passage is part of a record of the families of Benjamin, which enumerates the ancestors and their descendants. The name Schimeï, although common in biblical history (several characters bear it), designates here only one man, an ancestor of the Benjamite families mentioned.

sens: Man of Ramah in charge of King David's vineyards
H8096O.detail: Schimeï is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:27. He was a Ramathite (inhabitant of Ramah) and was responsible for overseeing the royal vineyards of King David. He was an administrator of the agricultural resources of the kingdom, tasked with ensuring wine production.
H8096O.origine: The name Schimeï (Hebrew שִׁמְעִי) literally means "he who is renowned" or "he who is heard of." It was a name borne by several characters in the history of Israel, particularly during the Davidic and post-exilic monarchy. The name likely reflects a figure of notoriety or reputation in its context.
H8096O.emploi: Schimeï appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 27:27, where he is identified as the officer in charge of the royal vineyards of King David. He appears in the list of administrators of the kingdom established by David to manage the various resources of the palace and royal estate. His role was specialized: overseeing wine production and managing the vineyards belonging to the crown. This position indicates that he was a person of recognized trust and competence.

sens: Levite, son of Heman and brother of Jehiel, who participated in the purification of the temple under King Hezekiah of Judah
H8096P.detail: Schimeï is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King Hezekiah undertakes to purify the temple of Jerusalem after years of religious neglect. He is identified as the son of the musician Heman, himself a renowned Levite, and the brother of Jehiel. His role in this religious reform shows the involvement of important Levitical families in the temple worship at the time of this major spiritual renewal (2 Chronicles 29:14).
H8096P.origine: The name Schimeï comes from a Hebrew root meaning "renowned" or "famous." It is a name borne by many people in the Old Testament, often associated with Levitical functions or temple ministries. The name can also be written Shimhi or Shimi in other biblical contexts.
H8096P.emploi: Schimeï appears only once in the preserved biblical texts, in 2 Chronicles 29:14. He is listed among the Levites who responded to King Hezekiah's call to sanctify the temple, probably between 715 and 686 BC. His appearance in this context of religious restoration underscores the importance of families of musician-priests in divine service.
H8096P.portee: The mention of Schimeï reminds us that the religious reforms of the faithful kings of Judah relied on the active participation of the Levites, guardians of worship and tradition. It invites the reader to see how God used these servants to restore the purity of the temple and revive the piety of the people.

sens: Levite brother of Conania, steward of the offerings and tithes of the temple during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah
H8096Q.detail: Schimeï is a Levite who lived during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah (8th century B.C.). He was the brother of Conania, and both worked together in the stewardship of the temple: Conania supervised the collection of voluntary offerings, tithes, and sacred objects, while Schimeï was his assistant or co-responsible (2 Chronicles 31:12-13). Along with other Levites like Jehiel, Azazia, and several others, they managed these precious goods according to the orders of the king and the chief of the house of God, Azaria.
H8096Q.origine: The name Schimeï means "renowned" or "he who hears." It is a common name among the Levites of the Old Testament. Several characters bear this name at different periods in the history of Israel, from the time of David to the time of Ezra, often holding religious or administrative positions.
H8096Q.emploi: Schimeï appears only twice in the Bible, both in 2 Chronicles 31:12-13, during the time of King Hezekiah. He is presented as a trustworthy Levite, brother and collaborator of Conania, charged with him with the stewardship of the temple's income — voluntary offerings, tithes, and sacred objects. This brief mention in a context of religious reform shows a responsible man working under the authority of the king and the chief priest to ensure the proper management of resources intended for worship.

sens: A Levite during the return from exile who had married a foreign woman
H8096R.detail: Schimeï is a Levite (member of the tribe of Levi, dedicated to the service of the temple) mentioned only once in the Bible, during Israel's return from exile in Babylon. He is among the men who, like many others at that time, had taken a non-Israelite wife, which was contrary to divine law. His name appears in Ezra 10:23 in the list of Levites who had to send away these foreign women to purify themselves and realign with God's will.
H8096R.origine: The name Schimeï means "renowned" or "he who is heard," derived from a Hebrew root related to fame or reputation. It is a name borne by several characters at different times in the history of Israel (a military officer of David, a supervisor of royal vineyards, various Levites, an ancestor of Mordecai), but this one specifically refers to the Levite of the return from exile attested in Ezra 10:23.
H8096R.emploi: Schimeï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:23. He is part of the Levites named in the register of men who had contracted mixed marriages during or after the Babylonian exile. Upon the return of the people to Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple, under Ezra's leadership, these marriages were deemed contrary to the law, and the foreigners had to be sent away. This mention shows that even the Levites, who were in the service of God, had succumbed to this transgression and needed to be reminded of obedience.

sens: A man from the time of the return from exile, mentioned only once
H8096S.detail: Schimeï is a name borne by several characters in the Old Testament at different periods, but in Ezra 10:33, it refers to a man who had married a foreign woman and had to separate from her during the return from exile under Ezra. This is an example among many Israelites who had to rectify their marital situation to respect the purity of the restored people.
H8096S.origine: The name Schimeï comes from a Hebrew root meaning "renowned" or "famous." It is a patronymic attested many times in the Old Testament, borne by men from various tribes and functions: Benjamites, Levites, Simeonites, Reubenites. The diversity of these bearers of the name reflects its popularity in ancient Israel.
H8096S.emploi: Schimeï appears only once in Ezra 10:33, in the list of men who had taken foreign wives and who accepted to send them away to conform to Ezra's request. This mention is set in the strict context of the return from exile in Babylon, where the reconstruction of the Israelite community required the renewal of its commitments to the Law.

sens: A man of the tribe of Levi at the time of Ezra
H8096T.detail: Schimeï is a Levite from the time of the return from exile, mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in Ezra 10:38 among the men who had married foreign women and who ended these unions at Ezra's command, during the religious and moral reorganization of Israel upon returning from Babylon.
H8096T.origine: The name Schimeï means "renowned" or "he who hears." It is a common Hebrew name in the Old Testament, borne by several different characters over the centuries: members of Saul's royal family during David's time, officers of King Solomon, Levites involved in temple worship, and other figures in Israel's history. Each bearer of this name represents a distinct era or role in God's people.
H8096T.emploi: Schimeï is a proper name borne by at least sixteen different people in the Hebrew Bible. The one mentioned here, in Ezra 10:38, lived during the time of the great religious reform led by Ezra after the return from Babylon around 458 B.C. He belongs to the group of Levites who had transgressed the Law by marrying non-Israelite women. Ezra, seeing this situation as a serious violation of the separation that Israel was to maintain from neighboring peoples, ordered the dissolution of these unions.

sens: Benjamite, father of Jair and grandfather of Mordecai during the time of Esther
H8096U.detail: Schimeï is an ancestor of Mordecai mentioned in the book of Esther. He is a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived before the Babylonian exile. His son Jair and his grandson Mordecai are the next generations of this same Benjaminite family. According to the genealogy given in Esther 2:5, Mordecai is "the son of Jair, the son of Schimeï, the son of Kish."
H8096U.origine: The name Schimeï means "renowned" or "he who is spoken of." It is a Hebrew name borne by many figures in the history of Israel, particularly among the Levites and Benjamites. The same name appears among worship leaders, royal administrators, and Levites at different times (under David, Solomon, Hezekiah, Ezra). In this case, he is the earliest ancestor of Mordecai whose name has been preserved.
H8096U.emploi: Schimeï appears only once in the Bible in the text that concerns us: in Esther 2:5, where he is identified as the son of Kish and the father of Jair in the genealogy of Mordecai. This mention in the context of the return from exile and the life of the Jews under Persian rule situates this Benjaminite family in post-exilic history. The name signifies that this family had some notoriety or importance in the Jewish community.

sens: Levite, son of Jahath and grandson of Gershon, living during the time of King David
H8096V.detail: 1. Schimeï is a Levite from the branch of Gershon, one of the three sons of Levi from whom the assistants of worship descended. He is mentioned as the son of Jahath and as an ancestor of Ethan, a temple musician (1 Chronicles 6:42). His name means "renowned" or "illustrious." 2. Schimeï also appears as a chief of a Levite family: his sons Shelomith, Haziel, and Haran led the paternal houses of the family of Laadan (1 Chronicles 23:9), responsible for the organization of worship and assisting the priests.
H8096V.origine: The name Schimeï comes from Hebrew and means "renowned" or "he who has fame." This name belonged to several important characters in the history of Israel, notably descendants of Levi charged with worship. In the Levitical genealogy, Schimeï represents a respectable branch of the temple assistants.
H8096V.emploi: Schimeï is mentioned twice in Chronicles, always in the context of Levitical genealogies and the organization of worship. In 1 Chronicles 6:42, he appears in the genealogical succession of Ethan the singer, ancestor of the temple musicians. In 1 Chronicles 23:9, his sons are listed as heads of families responsible for the maintenance of the tabernacle and the temple. These mentions situate Schimeï in the time of David and attest to the prominent role of his descendants in the religious services of Israel.

sens: Levite, son of Jeduthun, chief of the tenth division of singers during the time of King David
H8096X.detail: Shimei is a Levite from the time of King David, belonging to the musical family of Jeduthun. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 25:17 as the chief of the tenth division of the temple singers, with his sons and brothers forming a group of twelve musicians. His name means "renowned," which is fitting for a prominent musician serving in the temple worship.
H8096X.origine: The name Shimei (שִׁמְעִי in Hebrew) means "renowned" or "one who has a reputation." It is derived from a Hebrew root evoking fame or honor. This name was borne by several men in Israel at different times, including Levites involved in temple service and men from various tribes. In the biblical text, the name appears in several spelling variations (Shimei, Shimhi, Shimi).
H8096X.emploi: Shimei is mentioned only once in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 25:17, where he is presented as the son of Jeduthun and chief of the tenth division of the temple singers during David's time. This prestigious office shows that he was a high-ranking Levite, responsible for a significant portion of the temple's musical service. His group consisted of twelve musicians, indicating the importance of his role in the organization of public worship.
H8096X.portee: Shimei reminds us that the temple worship in Jerusalem was carefully organized and involved many dedicated servants. The temple singers were not a secondary group but played a central role in Israel's worship, highlighting the importance of praise and music in the spiritual life of God's people.

sens: Shimei, a man from the tribe of Levi during the Exodus and in the wilderness
the descendants of Shimei, forming a clan among the Levites
H8097.detail:
1. Shimei is a Levite from the lineage of Gershon, first mentioned in the Exodus: he is the son of Gershon and the brother of Libni. He is the father of several children including Jahath and Beriah.
2. The "Shimeites" (in plural) refer to the family or clan of the descendants of Shimei. In Numbers 3:21, this clan forms one of the two families of the Gershonites, the servants of the Lord at the tabernacle. In Zechariah 12:13, these families of Shimei are listed among the houses of Levi that will mourn with the Spirit of grace and supplication.
H8097.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew "Shimei" (שִׁמְעִי), which literally means "he has heard" or "renowned" — the idea of one whose reputation is known. The name appears in the genealogy of Levi, establishing an important line of descent among the ministers of worship.
H8097.emploi: This word designates both Shimei as a particular Levitical ancestor and his descendants as a group. Shimei the patriarch appears in the genealogical lists of the Levites (Exodus 6:17), and his descendants form one of the Levitical families organized for the service of the tabernacle. They are also found in the prophecies of Zechariah concerning the day of judgment and grace, where the families of Levi will play a role of repentance and intercession. The context remains that of divine service and holiness.

sens: Prophet of the Lord in the kingdom of Judah during the time of King Rehoboam
H8098A.detail: Shemaiah is a prophet who receives direct words from God at the critical moment when the united kingdom of Israel has just divided. When Rehoboam, king of Judah, wishes to march against the northern kingdom to reclaim it, God speaks to Shemaiah and commands him to stop the king and his troops (1 Kings 12:22; 2 Chronicles 11:2). Later, when the Egyptian pharaoh Shishak invades Judah, Shemaiah reminds the king that this defeat is a consequence of the people's unfaithfulness to the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:5). Then, seeing that the king and the leaders repent, he brings a message of hope: God will not destroy the kingdom and will come to its aid (2 Chronicles 12:7). Shemaiah embodies the faithful prophet who delivers God's word directly, whether it be one of prohibition, judgment, or consolation.
H8098A.origine: The name Shemaiah literally means "heard by the Lord" or "the Lord has heard," formed from the root "shamar" (to hear) and the divine name Yah. This name expresses the conviction that this prophet is one to whom God has granted His attention and through whom He makes His voice heard to the people. It is a prophetic name that reflects the very essence of Shemaiah's calling: to be the spokesperson for the one who hears the cries of His people.
H8098A.emploi: Shemaiah appears five times in the Bible, all mentions being found in 2 Chronicles and one echo in 1 Kings, all dating from the reign of Rehoboam (around 930 B.C.). He is a political prophet who intervenes in the major crises of the young kingdom of Judah: he prevents a civil war that Rehoboam might have triggered against northern Israel, then interprets the calamity of Shishak's invasion as divine judgment followed by grace (2 Chronicles 12:15 mentions him as the author of a chronicle). His successive interventions show a prophet attentive to the king's repentance and capable of modulating his message according to the people's actions. Shemaiah is also known as a chronicler, his writings being integrated into the official records of the kingdom.
H8098A.portee: Shemaiah teaches that the true prophet is one who speaks in the name of God with authority, without hesitation towards political power when necessary. His actions show that divine judgment is never final for those who repent: in the face of the humiliation of the king and the leaders, God withdraws His hand. For the believer, this message affirms that the Lord truly listens to those who cry out to Him and that He moderates His anger towards those who acknowledge their sin.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah, descendant of Zerubbabel
Prophet of the Lord during the time of King Rehoboam
False prophet during the time of Jeremiah
Several Levites and priests from the time of David to that of Nehemiah
H8098B.detail:
1. Shemaiah is first a man from the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy, whose genealogy is recorded in Scripture: son of Shecaniah and father of several children (Hattush, Jigeal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat), as shown in 1 Chronicles 3:22.
2. The name designates a prophet of the Lord who served during the time of King Rehoboam of Judah, bearing a divine message for the king and his people.
3. Under this same name appears a false prophet during the time of Jeremiah, called the Nehelamite, who deceived the people with false words supposedly prophetic.
4. The name Shemaiah also refers to several Levites and priests who served in the temple from the time of King David to that of Nehemiah, holding important roles in the worship and administration of God's people.
H8098B.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "heard by the Lord" (from "Shama" = to hear and "Yah" = the Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name and expresses trust in God's listening. This name was quite common in Israel, borne by about twenty-six different individuals mentioned in the Bible, especially among Levites and priests.
H8098B.emploi: Shemaiah is a name borne by more than twenty-five distinct characters in the Old Testament, from the time of David (tenth century) to that of Nehemiah (fifth century). Most are Levites or priests who play a role in temple worship or the administration of worship, particularly during the return from exile. Two figures stand out: an authentic prophet during the time of Rehoboam, and a false prophet during the time of Jeremiah, the Nehelamite. The frequency of the name among the clergy and genealogies reflects its prestige in Judah, linked to its spiritual significance of being "heard by the Lord." In the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 3:22, it is an important genealogical link in the descent of Zerubbabel and the royal house.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H8098C.detail: 1. Schemaeja is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:37. He is the father of Shimri and is listed in a genealogy during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms (Judah in the south, Israel in the north). His name literally means "heard by the Lord," expressing the confidence that God listens to and protects the one who bears this name.
H8098C.origine: The name Schemaeja comes from the Hebrew שְׁמַע (shama, "to hear") and יָהּ (Yah, abbreviated form of the divine name Lord). It belongs to a family of common theophoric names in Israel, that is, names incorporating the name of God. This same name was borne by several other biblical figures — notably a prophet during the time of King Rehoboam of Judah, and a false prophet during the time of the prophet Jeremiah — but this entry concerns only the man of Simeon mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:37.
H8098C.emploi: Schemaeja appears only once in the preserved biblical texts: in 1 Chronicles 4:37, where he is listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon. He is named as the father of Shimri, indicating that he was a recognized ancestor in this tribe. No additional details about his life, deeds, or role are provided — it is merely a genealogical insertion intended to establish the lineages of the descendants of Simeon.

sens: A man of the tribe of Reuben during the time of the divided monarchy
H8098D.detail: 1. Schemaeja is a member of the tribe of Reuben mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the son of Joel and the father of Gog, in a genealogy of the descendants of Reuben.
H8098D.origine: The name Schemaeja means "Heard by Jehovah" or "The Lord has heard": it reflects the belief that God listens to His people. This name was borne by many individuals in ancient Israel, particularly among the Levites, prophets, and leaders.
H8098D.emploi: Schemaeja of Reuben appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 5:4, as a link in a genealogical chain of the descendants of Reuben. Unlike other Schemaeja in the Old Testament — notably the prophet during the time of Rehoboam, or the false prophet during the time of Jeremiah — this one has no recorded story. He is simply listed in the genealogical register of God's people.

sens: Levite during the Exile and Return, son of Hashub
H8098E.detail: Schemaeja is a Levite mentioned twice in the Bible, always as the son of Hashub and a descendant of Azrikam and Hashabiah. In 1 Chronicles 9:14, he appears among the Levites listed during the return of the exiles. In Nehemiah 11:15, he is again cited in a similar list of Levites established in Jerusalem after the reconstruction of the Temple. These two occurrences most likely refer to the same man, serving the Temple and the restored community.
H8098E.origine: The name Schemaeja literally means "heard by Jehovah" or "God has heard," composed of the Hebrew "Shema" (to hear) and the divine name "Yah." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the belief that God listens to and responds to His people. Several other biblical figures bear this same name, including a prophet during the time of King Rehoboam and a false prophet during the time of Jeremiah.
H8098E.emploi: This Schemaeja is a Levite active during the crucial period of the restoration of the Jewish people after the Babylonian Exile. The two passages that mention him (1 Chronicles 9:14 and Nehemiah 11:15) are almost identical, indicating that the Ezra-Nehemiah tradition regarded him as an important figure in the Levitical clergy of his time. He is part of the Levites of the sons of Merari, a branch of the priesthood responsible for the maintenance of the Tabernacle and the Temple. His appearance in these official lists shows his role as a liturgist and worship leader in the restored community.

sens: Chief Levite during the time of King David, responsible for transporting the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem
H8098G.detail: Schemaeja is a Levite from the family of the sons of Elizaphan, mentioned as a chief (or one of the chiefs) during the solemn transport of the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem under the reign of King David. In 1 Chronicles 15:8, he is presented as "the chief and his brothers, two hundred," meaning he leads two hundred other Levites from his family. In 1 Chronicles 15:11, David calls him by name among the most important priests and Levites for this sacred mission, alongside Zadok, Abiathar, Uriel, Asaiah, and Joel. His role demonstrates the importance of this ceremony and the honor given to the Levites chosen for this service.
H8098G.origine: The name Schemaeja literally means "heard by the Lord" (from the Hebrew "shama" = to hear, and "Yah" = the Lord). This name expresses the confidence that the Lord answers the prayers and cries of His people. It was a common name among Levites and religious leaders in the Old Testament.
H8098G.emploi: Schemaeja is mentioned only in 1 Chronicles, in chapters 15, verses 8 and 11. He appears in the context of the reign of King David, during a major event: the transport of the Ark of the Covenant from its retreat to Jerusalem, the new religious capital of Israel. This event is a manifestation of King David's faith and the central importance of the divine presence for God's people. Schemaeja and his Levite brothers had the ritual responsibility of overseeing this sacred transport.
H8098G.portee: The role of Schemaeja reminds us that service to the Lord requires dedication, organization, and faithfulness. His name, which means "heard by the Lord," encourages the believer: the Lord hears those who serve Him sincerely. This figure also shows us that the worship of the true God has always required structure, leaders, and order, rather than chaos or improvisation.

sens: Name borne by several characters in the Old Testament, including a Levite scribe during the time of King David
H8098H.detail: Shemaiah is a proper name borne by many characters in the history of Israel. The character mentioned in 1 Chronicles 24:6 is Shemaiah, son of Nethaneel, who served as a secretary (scribe) to King David. He is cited in the context of organizing the families of the priests and Levites, to register them and proceed with the drawing of lots for the priestly duties.
H8098H.origine: The name Shemaiah means "heard by the Lord" (or "Jehovah has heard"), formed from the Hebrew "shmah" (to hear) and "Yah" (God). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the belief that God listens to and answers prayers. The name frequently appears in genealogies and biblical narratives to designate men from various tribes and functions.
H8098H.emploi: Shemaiah is a very common name in the Old Testament, borne by at least 26 different characters according to genealogies and biblical narratives. The Shemaiah of 1 Chronicles 24:6 is one of the most clearly identified by his functions: secretary or scribe of King David, responsible for recording and administratively organizing the priestly and Levitical families during the distribution of worship offices. Other Shemaiah are prophets, false prophets, Levitical musicians, or exiles returned from Babylon. The recurrence of the name shows that it was honorable and common among the Levites and ministers of worship.

sens: Son of Obed-Edom, Levite during the time of King David
H8098I.detail: Shémaja is a Levite, son of Obed-Edom, who lived during the time of King David. He is the firstborn mentioned in the list of Obed-Edom's children (1 Chronicles 26:4). He was a man of valor who had authority in his father's house (1 Chronicles 26:6). He himself had several sons, all valiant men, including Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, and Semaeja, who continued the lineage of distinguished Levites (1 Chronicles 26:7).
H8098I.origine: The name Shémaja means "heard by the Lord" in Hebrew: it is composed of the verb "to hear, to listen" and the divine name. It is a theophoric name (containing the name of God) common in ancient Israel, expressing the confidence that a prayer will be heard by the Lord. The name is borne by several different individuals in the Old Testament, but the usage here refers to a specific Levite from the time of David.
H8098I.emploi: The Shémaja mentioned in 1 Chronicles 26 is a Levite doorkeeper or guardian of the temple during the time of King David. He belongs to the family of the children of Obed-Edom, a lineage of Levites known for their strength and valor. The three verses that mention him place him in the context of the organization of temple services: his brothers and sons, all valiant men, are enumerated, who participated in the responsibilities of worship and guarding the sanctuary.

sens: Levite teacher during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah
H8098J.detail: Schemaeja is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:8, where King Jehoshaphat sends him on a mission with other Levites and priests to teach the Law in the cities of Judah. His name means "heard by the Lord," which expresses the Levite's relationship with God. He embodies the role of Levites as instructors and propagators of the knowledge of God among the people.
H8098J.origine: The name Schemaeja comes from Hebrew and literally means "heard by the Lord" (from "shama," to hear, and "Yah," the Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common for Levites and servants of Israelite worship. This type of name reflects piety and dedication to God.
H8098J.emploi: Schemaeja appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He is one of the Levites that King Jehoshaphat sends on an official mission: to teach the Law of the Lord in all the cities of Judah, accompanied by other Levites and priests. This mention places him at the heart of a major religious and educational reform. The context shows that Jehoshaphat, after strengthening his power, wishes to enhance the knowledge of God among his subjects by sending authorized instructors. Schemaeja thus represents the Levitical service in favor of the instruction of the people.
H8098J.portee: Schemaeja reminds the reader of the importance that God places on the teaching of His Word. Although this Levite accomplishes only one mission in the biblical text, his participation in this work of instruction shows that every servant of God, even one whose name is mentioned only once, has a role in passing on the faith to future generations. It is an invitation to see that every faithful participation in the service of God has value, even if it remains discreet.

sens: Levite, son of Jeduthun, living during the divided monarchy
H8098K.detail: 1. Schemaeja is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi dedicated to temple service. He is mentioned as the son of Jeduthun, a famous musician of the temple. This name appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:14, among the Levites listed during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah.
H8098K.origine: The name Schemaeja literally means "heard by the Lord" in Hebrew: it combines the idea of being listened to or heard by God. It is a theophoric name, bearing the divine name, which expresses confidence in the benevolent listening of the Lord. Several men have borne this name in the history of Israel, including a prophet during the reign of Rehoboam and a false prophet during the time of Jeremiah.
H8098K.emploi: Schemaeja is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 29:14. He is listed among the Levites during the time of King Hezekiah, who undertook a great religious reform and restoration of temple worship after a period of neglect. His appearance in this list testifies to his place among the temple servants, inheriting the musical and cultic function of his father Jeduthun.
H8098K.portee: This name reminds us that the Levites, although less visible than the priests, played an essential role in the religious life of Israel. Schemaeja represents a generation of temple servants who remained faithful to their charge, even in times of trial. His name also carries a message of trust: the Lord hears His servants.

sens: man from the tribe of Judah who distributed offerings to the priests and Levites during the reign of King Hezekiah
H8098L.detail: Schemaeja is a Hebrew name that designates a man responsible, in the priestly cities, for faithfully distributing the offerings to his fellow Levites. His name literally means "heard by the Lord." He appears in 2 Chronicles 31:15 where he is mentioned among those who managed the gifts brought to the worship of the Lord, a task requiring honesty and dedication.
H8098L.origine: The name Schemaeja comes from Hebrew "Shema" (to hear) and "Yah" (the Lord). It thus means "heard by the Lord" or "the Lord has heard." This type of theophoric name (which contains the divine name) was common in Israel to express the relationship between the person and God. Many individuals named Schemaeja appear in the Old Testament, from prophets to ordinary Levites.
H8098L.emploi: Schemaeja is mentioned only once in the Bible in the passage of 2 Chronicles 31:15. He lived during the time of King Hezekiah and served as a manager or distributor of the offerings brought to the temple in the priestly cities. He worked alongside other trustworthy men to ensure that the contributions of the faithful reached the priests and Levites faithfully and equitably, according to their respective divisions. His role reflects the administrative organization of worship in the kingdom of Judah.
H8098L.portee: Schemaeja's role illustrates the importance of integrity and faithfulness in divine service, even in material or administrative tasks. The mention of his name reminds us that God sees and recognizes those who serve Him with honesty and dedication, even if their ministry remains humble and discreet. Every task in the service of the Lord, great or small, counts in the eyes of God.

sens: Levite family leader during the reign of King Josiah of Judah
H8098M.detail: Schemaeja is a Levite who lived during the time of King Josiah of Judah. He appears in the account of the Passover celebrated during this reign, where he is among the chief Levites responsible for providing the sacrifices: with his brothers Conania and Nethaneel, he distributed to the other Levites five thousand lambs and five hundred oxen for the Passover (2 Chronicles 35:9). He was a man of responsibility in the temple worship.
H8098M.origine: The name Schemaeja comes from Hebrew and means "heard by the Lord" or "that Jehovah has heard." This name expresses the confidence that God has heard the prayer of the parents. It was a common name among Levites and religious leaders in Israel.
H8098M.emploi: Schemaeja appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 35:9. He is mentioned as one of the chief Levites who played an active role in temple worship. During the reign of Josiah, when a great Passover was celebrated in Jerusalem, Schemaeja and his brothers distinguished themselves by ensuring that the necessary flocks for the sacrifices were distributed to the Levites, thus demonstrating their dedication to the religious service of Israel.
H8098M.portee: This character reminds us of the essential role of the Levites in the religious life of Israel. The fact that Schemaeja and his brothers mobilized for a great celebration of the Passover shows how the worship leaders served the Lord with generosity and organization. It is a discreet yet edifying example of humble and faithful service in the work of God.

sens: Member of the family of Adonikam who returned from exile with Ezra
H8098N.detail: Schemaeja is one of the descendants of Adonikam who returned from Babylonian captivity with Ezra. His name appears in the list of family leaders and their sons who undertook the journey back to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:13). He is part of those Israelites who, after the exile, reconstituted the community of God's people in the promised land.
H8098N.origine: The name Schemaeja means "Heard by the Lord" or "Jehovah has heard" in Hebrew. It is formed from two elements: "shama" (heard, listened) and "Jah" (God). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the confidence that God hears the prayers of His people. Several individuals have borne this name throughout the history of Israel.
